dugout.hull.steeringProvenance: Steering is ATTESTED as a negative: the one measured performance row is a paddled crossing (Kaifu’s Sugime, Taiwan→Yonaguni, 2019), the polar’s own note reads “Paddled”, and nothing hung on the hull is attested anywhere this early. The paddle is crew gear, no crew is drawn, so the hull mounts nothing.

voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].heightMProvenance: RECORDED: the Polynesian Voyaging Society's specification graphic (hokulea.com/wp-content/uploads/hokulea-diagram.pdf, Dave Swann / Star-Advertiser for PVS; r262/hokulea-diagram.pdf): "Mast Height: 31ft, 2in" and "Spar Height: 41ft, 5in", both dimensioned on the profile from the deck line to the forward mast's head and to its yard's tip — 31 ft 2 in is 9.50 m, deck to masthead, on the forward mast. Read against the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px): the foremast's foot meets the deck at plate (405, 715) and its head — the top of the pole, where the shrouds and the halyard blocks gather and the yard stands on alone — at y 207 ± 6 (r262/fore-cap-8x.png), 508 px; at round 250's 52 ± 2 px/m that is 9.8 ± 0.4 m, and the record's 9.50 m pins the plate's scale at the rig to 53.5 ± 1 px/m (the hull's manu tips read 54 at the near hull; the rig stands on the centreline). Before round 262 the record gave both masts 0.95 of Steel's main, 9.05 m — a warship's rule of 1794 on a Hawaiian double canoe whose owner publishes the height. Round 262.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].masthead.provenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px) at 8x, at the 53.5 ± 1 px/m the foremast's recorded 9.50 m pins at the rig (round 262); r263/fore-head-fit-8x.png and main-head-fit-8x.png, contrast-stretched crops with a 5 px grid (a cell is 0.09 m). On BOTH poles: at the head a short stiff piece, pale on the fore and dark on the main, whose top is at the masthead and whose lower end stands 6–8 px (0.11–0.15 m) proud of the pole's forward face about 20 px (0.37 m) down — a horn or cheek leaning forward at its foot, its function not readable; under it, on the forward face, a column of pale rounded blocks, each 6–8 px (0.11–0.15 m), the first about 18 px (0.34 m) under the head and the last about 63–83 px (1.2–1.55 m) under it (fore y 225–290 under a head at 207; main y 295–340 under a head at 277), four on each pole at this scale (± 1: two may be one, or a seizing may read as a block); the shrouds fan down and forward from the column. Nothing stands on the AFTER face, where the yard lies lashed (round 261). The blocks' functions (the halyard, the shrouds' or the sheet's tackles) are not readable off the plate and are not named; the count, the size and the band they occupy are the read. Round 263.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudsProvenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px) at the 53.5 ± 1 px/m the foremast's recorded 9.50 m pins at the rig (round 262): r264/plate-fore-landings-3x.png (x 150–430, y 380–860, contrast-stretched, a 10 px grid) and plate-rig-2x.png. From the fore masthead a fan of pale lines runs down and forward over the sky to the near hull's rail — a directional sweep of the plate from the head (r264, lines scored by their mean brightness over the sky between y 350 and 690) finds five or six, with x at y 700 of about 267, 285, 355, 375, 381 and 388 — of which the two nearly along the pole (381, 388) are the halyard's fall and the pole's own edge, and one is the forestay to the bow; and two or three more cross the fore sail's cloth from the head down and aft. Four a side, ± 1: the near hull's lines forward and aft of the mast less the stay and the fall. The main's fan crosses the fore sail and reads the same count with the same ± 1 (r264/plate-main-shrouds-grid-4x.png). Which line lands on which beam end the plate does not resolve — crew stand along the rail in front of the landings — so the model keeps the lashing class's rule: each shroud takes its own beam, the four nearest the mast. Before round 264 the record carried 2 a side, a class figure, with the plate's excess noted since round 247. Round 264.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudSetupProvenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px, about 50 px/m at the near hull): every shroud from each masthead lands on the hull's rail at a beam end, none on the platform, and the vessel carries no metal fastening (her own construction row), so the set-up is a lashing round the beam at the rail. The count a side is read in shroudsProvenance (round 264). The fitting at the foot — a hardwood bullseye with the lanyard rove through it — is read in shroudFoot (round 265); the hole's height over the timber the lanyard wraps is read in shroudFoot.holeOverSeatM (round 266), at the one foot the deck plate shows down to its timber.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudHead.provenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px) at 8x, 53.5 ± 1 px/m at the rig (round 262); r264/plate-fore-head-eyes-8x.png and plate-main-head-eyes-8x.png (contrast-stretched crops with a 5 px grid, a cell 0.09 m). The shrouds do not leave the pole at its head: they converge on its forward side in a band y 265–300 under a head at 207 (1.1–1.7 m under the head, ± 0.2 m — a 10 px read at each edge of the band), the lower part of the block column round which they fan (round 263). Their fastening at the pole — an eye in each shroud seized round the pole, a pair to a seizing, or a collar the shrouds are hitched to — is not readable at this scale; the model draws one rope collar round the pole for each pair, the forward pair highest and the after pair lowest, a class order read from no plate. Before round 264 the class ended every shroud 0.03 of the pole's height under its head, on the axis. Round 264.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].atProvenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px; the near hull's manu tips at x 128 and 1140 span her 18.7 m, 54 px/m, and her waterline runs x 155 to 1125): the foremast's foot meets the deck at x 405, (405 − 155) / 970 = 0.26 of the waterline from the stem. A 10 px read is 0.01 of u. Before round 249 the record stepped ONE mast at 0.46, between the two the plate shows and the card's own Rig row names. Round 249 read the foremast about 10.0 m and the mainmast about 11.7 m from deck to head off this plate and left the model's 9.05 m for both (a 0.95 share of Steel's main). Round 262 found the 11.7 m was the main YARD's tip at (697, 122) taken for the masthead, and set both heights: heightM and heightMProvenance.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].rakeProvenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px; 54 px/m at the near hull, about 50 at the far, so 52 ± 2 on the centreline where the rig stands): the foremast's foot at plate (405, 715) and its head at (410, 215), the mainmast's at (683, 725) and (690, 280) — both within a degree of vertical. The 6 was a class figure. Round 250; before it the model raked both masts 6° aft.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].diaMProvenance: READ off the 2009 broadside at 8x (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px, 52 ± 2 px/m at the rig; r261/z-fore-mid-8x.png): the fore mast at mid-height is about 10 px thick, 0.19 ± 0.04 m at that scale, a 2 px read; the main reads the same within it. Before round 261 the class drew both masts from the single hull's 1.05 m beam, 0.068 m thick at the foot — a 9 m pole with the girth of an oar. Round 261.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].sail.provenance: READ off the 2009 broadside (Wikimedia Commons, Hokule'aSailing2009.jpg, 1280 px; 54 px/m at the near hull, about 50 at the far, so 52 ± 2 on the centreline where the rig stands): the fore tack at plate (430, 715), the yard's tip at (425, 52) and the boom's tip at (760, 350) — the yard 663 px = 12.8 m at 90.4° over the aft-horizontal (the mast within a degree of vertical, so the yard lies along it, its peak above the masthead), the boom 492 px = 9.5 m at 48°, the spars opening 43°; the tack 0.5 m abaft the mast's foot at the deck. The cloth's head reaches the yard's tip. leechRatio 0.88 is the fore sail's cloth counted in pixels (96974) over its straight triangle (110308), the leech's hollow; the main is occluded by the fore and takes the same share. A 2 px/m scale error is 4% of length and 8% of area. Round 249 read the main's boom tip (990, 415) as the fore's, which is where its 64° spread and 12 m spars came from; the fore boom ends at (760, 350), just abaft the mainmast. tackUp 0.2 m is a class figure for the lashing over the deck, not a read. Before round 250 the class put the tack 0.22 L forward of the mast and solved 10.8 m spars at 42° from 25 m² a sail. Round 261 re-read the yard's PLACE at 8x (r261/z-fore-mid-8x.png, z-fore-head-8x.png, z-fore-deck-8x.png): the yard lies against the mast's after face from its heel to the masthead, lashed to it at the heel, at mid-height and at the head, about 6 px = 0.11 m thick against the mast's 10 px = 0.19 m, and stands on above the masthead as a free spar. The 0.5 m tackAbaft and the 1.0° yardOffMast of round 250 were the read of the cloth's corner at (430, 715) and of an angle inside the read's own ±0.9°, and are retired: the builder stands the yard at the two radii (the mast's radius plus the yard's) dead aft of the axis, the tack at the yard's heel, and the audit reads the offset and the lashings off the drawn spars. Round 262 re-scaled the spar reads from 52 to 53.5 ± 1 px/m — the scale the foremast's recorded 9.50 m (PVS, 31 ft 2 in) pins at the rig, inside round 250's 52 ± 2 — so the same pixel reads give the fore yard 663 px = 12.39 m, the boom 492 px = 9.20 m, the cloth to the yard's tip; the angles are scale-free. tipOverHeadM is the yard's tip over the masthead as the plate reads it: (207 − 52) / 53.5 = 2.90 m on the fore (the PVS graphic's 41 ft 5 in spar less its 31 ft 2 in mast is 3.12 m); the model's yard from its tack at tackUp over the deck puts the tip 3.09 m over the head, inside both reads. A 1 px/m scale error is 2% of length and 4% of area; a 6 px read of a masthead is 0.11 m.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudFoot.holeOverSeatPro: READ off the 2010 deck plate (Wikimedia Commons, 'Hokulea deck and sleeping area.JPG', 4000 × 2672 px; r265/crop-deck-2-x1700.png and crop-deck-3-x2550.png, the plate's x 1700–3550 and y 1000–1700 at 1.5x). At the NEAREST foot (plate x 2300–2700) the lanyard's three falls hang straight down from the hole to a fore-and-aft timber at the beam's lashing and wrap it, the same rope thickness top to bottom, so the heart and the timber are at one depth and the shroud's own rope scales both: 800 ± 160 px/m (20 px for a one-inch line). The hole's centre stands 505 ± 20 px at 1.5x — 337 px on the plate — over the top of the wrapped timber: 0.42 m ± 0.10 vertically, 0.45 m along the shroud's 20° lean, which is what the model's lash sets. The TWO FARTHER feet (plate x 3000–3300, about 3.6 times the nearest heart's distance, their hearts 80 px long) hang with their holes roughly 0.75 m over the waist-high rail below them and their lanyards run more than a metre down behind the rail's canvas before the plate loses them, so those two stand higher over their timber than the nearest one and by an unread amount; a lanyard's length is whatever the shroud's made length leaves, so the height need not be one figure for every foot. The record carries the nearest foot's read as the height for every foot; which feet stand higher is not readable (which beam each shroud takes, 0y⁴⁵, is not either). Before round 266 the model's height was the class figure 0.3 B (0.315 m), and round 265's read of the nearest hole 0.09 m over 'the cap rail' was a projection — that rail stands behind the heart at 3.6 times its distance, so a like height reads lower on the plate. Round 266.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudFoot.provenance: READ off the Marine Education Training Center series of 18 May 2010 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Hokulea deck and sleeping area.JPG', 4000 × 2672 px, CC BY-SA 3.0, Hōkūleʻa moored at Honolulu Community College with her crew off, the near hull's rail seen from the pier between the masts; r265/metc-2010-deck-sleeping.jpg, crops r265/crop-deck-*.png at 1.5x and crop-bullseye-3x.png), with the same fitting at every foot in 'front with masts', 'front and sleeping area', 'head on' and 'stern from side' of the same series (r265/metc-2010-*.jpg). Every shroud ends in a HARDWOOD BULLSEYE — a teardrop heart with one large hole, the shroud's end seized round the groove of its rim — and a lanyard of the shroud's half thickness rove through the hole in three or four falls down to the crossbeam's end at the rail, the tail coiled and hung on the shroud. The scale is the shroud's own rope: 20 px thick on the nearest heart (plate x 2300–2700, y 1050–1450), taken as a one-inch three-strand line, 25 ± 5 mm, so 800 ± 160 px/m there; the heart is 290 px long and 177 wide, 0.36 × 0.22 m ± 0.07, its lower tip about 0.14 m below the cap rail's top and its hole 0.09 m over it on that foot, the pair at plate x 3000–3300 standing about 0.3 m clear of the cap; its thickness is unread (the plates are face-on) and the model's 0.05 m is a class figure. Which beam each shroud takes is NOT read from these plates: the deck plate is a perspective along the rail from abeam of the fore mast and the bow-quarter plates foreshorten the rail, so a foot's station cannot be placed against a beam's without a scaled plan (0y⁴⁵ stands). The 2019 plate 'Hōkūleʻa mast.jpg' (Commons, 4608 px) shows WIRE shrouds converging at the head on a metal fitting: that is the rig after the 2012–13 dry-docking for the worldwide voyage, not the 2009 rig the model draws. Before round 265 the lashing class ended every shroud in a rope eye 0.3 B over the beam, a class figure read from no plate. Round 265.

Every shroud ends in a HARDWOOD BULLSEYE — a teardrop heart with one large hole, the shroud's end seized round the groove of its rim — and a lanyard of the shroud's half thickness rove through the hole in three or four falls down to the crossbeam's end at the rail, the tail coiled and hung on the shroud. The scale is the shroud's own rope: 20 px thick on the nearest heart (plate x 2300–2700, y 1050–1450), taken as a one-inch three-strand line, 25 ± 5 mm, so 800 ± 160 px/m there; the heart is 290 px long and 177 wide, 0.36 × 0.22 m ± 0.07, its lower tip about 0.14 m below the cap rail's top and its hole 0.09 m over it on that foot, the pair at plate x 3000–3300 standing about 0.3 m clear of the cap; its thickness is unread (the plates are face-on) and the model's 0.05 m is a class figure.
