panokseon.hull.sangjangProvenance: The CLOSED wall band between the gunwale and the fighting deck is attested: her own plate — the late-Joseon jeonseon drawing on this card, in the Gakseon dobon manner — closes the band with a painted plank belt on both sides she shows, and Hong Sun-jae (2025) reconstructs the same pangpae planking; the card's own Decks row calls the oar deck protected. The PORT ROW is read off that plate: a line of small square ports under the deck line, about sixteen a side at the plate's roughly 12 px/m — good to plus or minus two, no finer, and that bound is the drawing's, not the ship's. The dragon painted along the belt and the row of shields along the bulwark top in the same drawing are not drawn here; that simplification is recorded. Since round 142 the port row is OPENINGS: each port is cut through the drawn belt with jamb, sill and head reveal faces the plank's own gauge deep and a dark board a hand inboard, so it reads into the oar deck's shadow from every outboard bearing; before that each was a dark plate laid proud on the belt's face.
panokseon.hull.towerProvenance: The FORM is attested: the Gakseon dobon jeonseon drawing — the late-Joseon plate this card's own image follows — draws the janggundae as an open pavilion on the fighting deck: a railed platform on posts under a hipped roof standing clear above the bulwarks, the commander visible from the whole squadron. The PLAN is derived: no panokseon survives, so the 3.2 m square, the 2.6 m platform height and the roof pitch are read off that drawing at ship scale — good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The ladder, the baluster spacing and every scantling are reconstruction: a pavilion whose platform can be reached and whose rails land on its own columns, drawn at the joinery any standing structure needs; the plate attests none of it piece by piece.
panokseon.hull.portProvenance: The PORTS are attested for the class: the panokseon's chongtong stood on the fighting deck and fired through its plank bulwark — the gunners loading behind cover is the argument of the walled deck itself, and her card's Guns row carries the attested battery. The COUNT AT THE WALL, SIZE and SILL HEIGHT are derived: no example survives, the late-Joseon jeonseon plate on her card resolves the sangjang band's port row but not the fighting-deck wall's, and six a side is the drawn split of the recorded dozen-plus pieces. Each port is drawn 0.52 m square with its sill 0.14 m over the fighting deck — low, so the muzzle clears its own timber bed. Since round 141 the ports are OPENINGS cut through the drawn plank, with reveal faces the plank's own thickness deep and a dark board behind each so the port frames its muzzle in shadow; before that each was a dark plate laid on the wall's face with the barrel passing through solid plank.
panokseon.hull.anchorProvenance: The 닻 the warship plate itself draws: her navy's album, the Gakseondobon (c. 1797), lists mast, anchor [碇], oars and rudder on the 전선 plate (encykorea E0000455) — the anchor's presence is the album's own, one step more direct than the horong, which the album carries only on the grain-ship plate. The FORM is the tradition's, a NAVY-TRADITION EXTENSION stated here: the West Sea composite of oak shank (닻채), hook-arms hung both sides (닻가지), and a long grooved rectangular anchor-stone (닻돌) lashed on, because oak alone will not sink — the stone serving as the stock, 석제 닻장 in the report's own words. The type is RECORDED on her own coast: 154 anchor stones off Taean and Incheon, 2008–2019, rope grooves cut for the lashing, the wooden anchors found with them radiocarbon-dated from the 2nd century BC through Joseon — her own dynasty inside the run (Korea Heritage Service 2021). The stone is RECORDED since r201, the excavated object at its own size (the r199 rule): 진도Ⅳ-58 / 명량21-17, raised from the Myeongnyang strait's grid D10 on 14 August 2021 and catalogued at 166 × 53 × 29 cm, 458 kg, its lashing grooves cut top and bottom — 폭 7 × 깊이 2.5 cm and 11 × 3.5 cm — and its rim dressed (치석) toward the rectangle (『진도 명량대첩로 해역 수중발굴조사 보고서 Ⅳ』 2024, p. 147; caption verified against the plate's own photographs on the rendered page, r200). It is the largest Korean lashed-form stone in any report fetched here, raised from the same water that gave the class its arm, and it sits inside the corpus's own large band — Hong 2012's 대형군, 304–590 kg / 146–263 cm, the classification the 2021 Mado report itself applies (its footnote 64) — replacing the exhibition threshold this record cited through r200 ('over 2 m, 300–700 kg', Taean 2021). The band's ceiling runs to 590 kg, so larger stones are attested in the corpus; none fetched carries its own catalogue entry above 458, and that gap is stated. At 458 kg the stone is a load the drawn four-man horong breaks out at its bars' purchase. The ARMS take the form study's own count and splay (r196): TWO — every stock-anchor Hong 2013 draws carries two (그림 16 forms A–D, the stone-stock schematic 그림 17, and all six artifact reconstructions on p.135), and the institute's reconstruction figure draws two limbs at staggered whipped stations. The pre-r196 four came from the Standard Korean Dictionary's '보통 네 갈고리이며 두 갈고리도 있다' — CONTESTED here: the study reserves the many-hooked form for the STOCKLESS anchor (its E, whose modern analogue it names in 그림 18, a four-claw grapnel), never the stock anchor this record draws. SPLAY is MEASURED, 0.38 rad from the shank — the mean of six limb chords read tip-to-root at 300 DPI (그림 16 (A) 22°/27°, (C) 19°/26°, the institute figure ~19°/17°; the 17–27° spread is the audit band) — replacing the pre-r196 drawn 0.78, twice any plate. The ARM TIMBER is RECORDED (r197): 진도-641, the lashed tradition's one recovered wooden arm published with dimensions (the board's 2025 송호리1호선 report prints a second dimensioned anchor timber — a whole one-piece oak half of the two-shank insert form, 149.5 cm — a different form, named below) — raised off Jindo's Myeongnyang strait, zone C, 3 September 2013, and catalogued in 『진도 명량대첩로 해역 수중발굴조사 보고서 Ⅰ』 (국립해양문화재연구소 2015, p. 467; fetched whole from the institute's report board): 길이 190 cm, 너비 19.6 cm, 두께 40 cm, oak (수종분석: 상수리나무류). The catalogue's measured drawing reproduces its own printed numbers against the 1 m bar at 8.79 px/cm — plans 188.7/189.0 cm long and 19.2/20.7 cm wide, side envelope 40.7 cm — so the plate supports centimetre precision and the class draws the arm at the record: the whole timber, root to carved point, 1.90 m, section 0.196 m, replacing the pre-r197 drawn defaults (hook limb 1.2, section 0.12). The 두께 40 is the root crook's side envelope — the timber sweeps up where it met the shank — and the drawn frame keeps the institute figure's straight crossed timbers, the curve named. The species is not the tradition's only one: the strait's second arm — 진도Ⅱ-328, a 59.4 × 9.2 cm fragment raised 5 June 2017, the catalogue's own 목제닻을 구성하는 일부분 (보고서 Ⅱ 2018, p. 336) — analyses as zelkova (느티나무; the report's species appendix names its sample by the same date and grid), so the tradition built its arms in at least two hardwoods; a broken remnant, it tests nothing the class draws, and 진도-641 stays the only whole-run record. CONTESTED, the joint: 진도-641's two peg stations sit 0.35–0.55 m from its lap-notched root end, the economy of Hong's foot-rooted variant, not the drawn crossed frame's ~0.79 m derived blunt limb; the institute's frame stays the drawn one (r194's declared source), the artifact's own stations carried here. The Gwangyang arm (artifact ⑥) remains undimensioned in print — the form study's catalogue is qualitative and a reported find has no excavation report; its plain white photo rod anchors no scale. VARIANT NAMED: Hong's own plates root the arms at the foot with carved points rising to the stock's height, while the institute's figure crosses them whipped at 0.35 with points down and blunt ends bracing the stone — the drawn frame follows the institute's, the study's variant stated. The SHANK is DERIVED (r195): about 3.3 m on the 1.66 m stone, by the institute figure's own stone/shank proportion 0.51 (measured on the press-kit reconstruction at 3x, r194/r195), with the mechanism named in the form study the report itself cites — 홍광희 2013, 「전통 나무닻의 생김새 연구」, 『해양문화재』 6, pp. 107–143 (국립해양문화재연구소; fetched whole from the institute's own journal board, r195): the wooden anchor's shank was made LONG against oak's buoyancy, with the stock set at the arms' top height, not at the cable end where a modern anchor wears it. By that same study the pre-r195 crossbar is REMOVED: it sat at the modern head station the study explicitly distinguishes from the tradition's, and beside a stone stock the study argues a wooden 닻장 is redundant and draws none — the institute's reconstruction figure draws none either. CONTESTED, the study's own footnote 8: some hold that stock and stone were fitted together so the stone could not spin on a round shank — named here, not drawn. The crossings are pinned with two treenails each: the 19th-century 표민대화 anchor is drawn with two 나무못 at the joint, and both separately-made arms so far recovered (Jindo; Gwangyang Seonso) carry two square peg holes apiece — the study's artifacts ④ and ⑥. The stone's station and the frame are the institute's own reconstruction now (r194): the 2023 report 『한국의 닻돌』 (국립해양문화재연구소, 연구보고서 vol. 3, 195 pp., fetched whole from the CHA publications board, nttId 87406) names lashing to the shank's OUTSIDE (닻채 외부에 묶는 방식) the leading use for the plank-form stones, and carries the 19th-century 『표민대화』 fixing the stone at the shank's MIDDLE — 닻채 중앙부, held there by a 방살 pin through the shank (the pin is that book's own device; the drawn lashing is rope alone and the variant is named here). The institute's reconstruction figure (닻돌 구성, its Dec 2023 press release, fetched at 583×674 px — an unscaled illustration, proportions only) draws the crossed-arm frame whipped at the shank, blunt upper arm ends bracing the stone's underside, a spreader board across the splay, and the stone's centre at 0.57 of the shank above the foot; drawn at 0.55, band ±0.12 carrying the illustration's precision and the head-call (V-WSTATION audits the drawn station). The lashing follows the institute's reproduction as the 2021 exhibition poster photographs it: end turns seated in the stone's own rope grooves, crossed frapping over the midbody. The drawn rig is the one that HELD at sea (r196, mined from the thesis behind the study — 홍광희 2012, 조선대, fetched r195): in the thesis's own anchoring trials off Taean (표 8; 5–20 m of water, 30 m of cable, three runs per rig), only the stone lashed athwart the shank's middle anchored the boat — all three runs, at 33, 62 and 78 m — while the bare wooden anchor, the stone hung at the head and the stone hung on the cable failed all nine runs between them; the head rig floats the anchor so the arms cannot reach bottom (표 11's own reading), and the trial notes the wooden stock did little beside the stone — the crossbar's removal (r195) confirmed in the water. The cable-hung stone the thesis keeps as a plausible AUXILIARY for strong current, a second small stone bent to the cable — named here, not drawn. CONTESTED, the report's own sentence: no stone has been confirmed still lashed to its shank (닻돌이 닻채에 묶인 상태로 확인된 사례가 없어 추측만) — the station is the record's reconstruction, not a find; the boatwright's Chinese cognate (마광남, 배목수이야기 42) stands beside it. The one stone recovered still JOINTED to its timber (마도해역-212, raised articulated 2014, 2017 시굴보고서) is the Chinese two-shank INSERT form, pegged through mortised battens — a different joint, so the Korean lashed form's sentence stands (r199) — and that insert form is now attested aboard a Korean-built Goryeo coaster (송호리1호선, Haenam, hull dated AD 1021–1158, excavation report 2025: one oak half, 149.5 cm printed, stowed inside the hull), so the form crossed hull traditions without touching the lashed form's own evidence. Stow is PLACEMENT INFERENCE, the fleet rule: under way the anchor lies recovered on the open foredeck beside its own horong, rolled so no member stands upright, the cable bent at the head and led to the barrel. The boatwright's trip-ring and buoy are a fishing practice with no warship warrant — not drawn. No fetched source draws a 16th-century warship's anchor directly; the album is two centuries after her and the gap is stated. One more drawn witness in her own line since r206: the 문헌편's plates chapter (국립해양유산연구소, 학술총서 91집, pdf p. 143) reproduces the 귀선도 — two ink drawings of the roofed ship, 개인 소장 (최순선), on deposit with the 국가유산청 현충사관리소, undated in its caption — and both hang an anchor from the hull's end on a steeply angled shank with two curved arms crossing at the crown. In the two-masted drawing that end is unambiguously the BOW, beside the dragon head — the placement the drawn machine follows, against the encyclopedia's stern-drum variant named above; the roofed side view hangs the same form below its arched end-housing, and which end that housing caps is not resolved. The reproduction bounds the read: the ship spans about 1,500 px on the 300-dpi page — roughly 50 px/m if she is near the 도설's scale — and the anchor about 200 px, so the two-armed crossed form and the bow station are legible and nothing finer: no stone, no lashing, no stock can be affirmed or denied at that scale.
panokseon.hull.windlassProvenance: The horong (호롱, 揚錨機), the Korean tradition's bow anchor-windlass — a NAVY-TRADITION EXTENSION, stated here, not a ship attestation: her own attestation is generated, and no fetched source puts a windlass on a 16th-century warship directly. The machine is attested three ways in her line. Her navy's own album, the Gakseondobon (c. 1797), carries it on the grain-ship plate: the National Maritime Heritage Institute's 2011 reconstruction of that plate (24 m) sets the horong at the bow, and the launch record says the horong was recreated from the drawing. The institute's component classification of the excavated Goryeo ships lists the horong among the anchoring gear (정박구: 닻, 호롱, 닻돌, 엄말) — read in the institute's site excerpts; the carrying page was not pinned, and no claim is made that a wreck preserved a horong timber. The living tradition gives the machine's working: a drum with two long bars passed through at different points, crossed, four men at the ends, about one coil of cable wound on (옛 돛단배의 언어 3). The album's warship plate draws the anchor; whether it also draws the windlass is NOT established by the sources fetched. CONTESTED placement: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture's hanseon description fixes an anchor-winding drum at the STERN board beside the rudder; the drawn machine follows the naval line's build record, at the bow. Station u 0.10 is a PHOTO/TEXT read, +/-0.05 (the open foredeck abaft the stem, forward of the sangjang's drawn leading edge at u 0.16; the launch photo resolves about 19 px/m — form only, no dimension can be read from it). Barrel 2.7 m is a GEOMETRIC class default: the drawn deck is 4.7 m wide at the drawn station, the probe's own measure re-run r208 — it was 3.8 across the 5.79 m foredeck the 9.4 m shell drew, and when the shell came in to the record's ~7.6 m the barrel followed its own warrant, the deck it stands on, at the same side margins. Diameter 0.5 m, the 0.30 m underside and the two standards are Falconer 1769 CLASS DEFAULTS cross-tradition, as the cog (r173) and the junk (r174); the 2.0 m bars are a CLASS DEFAULT (0.75 m of grip beyond the drum each side, resting near-horizontal as the replica photo shows them left). throughBars is the tradition's own form read, replacing Falconer's single-ended handspikes for this record alone.
panokseon.hull.jeonseoProvenance: The 이충무공전서 권수 도설's 귀선지제 (1795), read whole at 300 dpi from the institute's own print — 국립해양유산연구소, 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 문헌편』 (전통 선박 조선 기술 Ⅷ, 학술총서 91집; fetched whole r205 from the institute's report board, nttId 4452, 127,831,863 bytes byte-exact; the volume is a pure image scan, zero fonts, so every read is a plate read), pdf pp. 121–123, hanmun and translation both on the page. The spec, entire: 저판(본판) 10 planks, 64자 8치 long, 12자 head / 14자 5치 waist / 10자 6치 tail; 현판(삼판) 7 a side, 7자 5치 high, lowest 68자 to topmost 113자, all 4치 thick; 노판 (bow transom) 4 planks 4자 high, a 현자포 hole each side through the second; 축판 (stern transom) 7 planks 7자 5치 high, 14자 5치 over 10자 6치, the sixth plank pierced 1자 2치 for the rudder (속명 치); 신방 rails, 가룡 crossbeams yoked at the bow 'like an ox's chest', 방패 bulwark 4자 3치 rail to rail; 개판(귀배판) 11 planks a side meeting scale-fashion with a 1자 5치 spine gap to raise and strike the masts; turtle head 4자 3치 × 3자, burning sulphur and saltpetre for smoke; 10 oars and 22 gunports a side with 12 doors; under-deck 24 rooms — 2 iron stores, 3 magazines, 19 crew berths — and a cabin each side above for captain and officers. The 좌수영 variant is printed as differences: 尺度長廣 與統制營龜船略同 — 'length and breadth about the same' — a 鬼頭 carved under the turtle head, 龜紋 painted on the cover, two doors a side, per-side gunhole counts 2/1/10/6, and 8 oars a side. THREE BOUNDS, the record's own: the editor states no earlier source recorded dimensions; states the 1795 통제영 ship differs from 충무공's original by 치수의 가감 — the numbers are the late dockyard ship's, two centuries after Myeongnyang; and the 도설 compares turtle ship to turtle ship only — the panokseon is named nowhere in it, so these numbers reach this card only through the roofing argument the card's own text carries. The foot is CONTESTED in the scholarship — 영조척 ~31.2 cm against 주척 ~20.8 — and both conversions are printed in the row. The 도설 text names NO ground tackle — no 닻, no 호롱 — so the anchor and windlass warrants on this card stand on the album, the excavations and the living tradition, unchanged by this read. A SECOND MEASURED RECORD in the same line since r208: the card's 1882 row is read from the 『각사등록』 통제영계록, Gojong 19 (1882), the 광서 정월 15일 승정원 개탁 entry — 一戰船 本板 長九十尺·廣十八尺·元高十一尺·船頭廣十五尺·船尾廣十二尺, 上粧 長一百五尺·廣三十九尺; 龜船 本板 長六十七尺·廣十三尺·元高十三尺·船頭廣十尺·船尾廣八尺, 上粧 長八十八尺·廣三十三尺; the 右別船 between them at 본판 67척 3촌 — read whole at 300 dpi from the same 문헌편's pdf pp. 135–137, hanmun and the volume's own Korean translation both on the page and agreeing column for column, and cross-checked against Hong 2025's 표 3, which sets the 1882 일전선 beside the 각선도본 전선 within 촌s. The register names no foot; the card's row prints both conversions, the 1795 row's own contest. THE 본문편 READ, r209 — 국립해양유산연구소, 『거북선 학술 복원 보고서 본문편』 (전통 선박 조선 기술 Ⅷ, 학술총서 91집, 2026; attachment /2 of the same board post, nttId 4452, 784,858,884 bytes byte-exact, 404 pages, image-only, so every read is a plate read; landed r208): pp. 110–112, the 통제영 turtle ship's hull form and structure. The report builds that ship on the 판옥선-line warship's flat-bottom construction, gives the bottom a 밑들기 rise of about 1.2척 at the bow and 1.0척 at the stern with the mid-body flat, keeps the upper deck's sheer gentle for the guns and the oars, and draws the body plan (그림 67) with the 상장 33척 wide over an upper hull 27척 wide, 3척 a side; 표 6 fixes 상요광 27 as the upper deck plank's mid breadth, 선요고/현요고 9.0/7.5 and 전고 20.5척, and the 기본 설계도 (p. 128) prints its foot: 1척 = 31.22 cm, the 영조척. The report's own bounds, from its 일러두기 (p. 2): the 도설 is a compilation two centuries after the war; the design is a reference model that tests functional possibility, not the original; and every drawing is an inferred design, not a measured one. That is the warrant behind the card's Beam row sentence on the 3척 overhang — a class witness from the institute's design, not a measurement of any ship. pp. 41–42, the 이순신 종가 귀선도: two drawings in private hands on deposit at 현충사, undated, in the 도설's own manner and put at about 1800; the report reads them as the 도설's image carried on in family transmission, not independent evidence, and their inscription's dimensions (bottom 10파, breadth 5파, length 13파) as a later rough understanding. pp. 44–45, the turtle-ship painting first shown in New York in 2004 (176 × 240 cm on silk, private): its inscription quotes the 1823 해동역사 almost verbatim, its firearms are 19th-century types, and its paint shows reworking, so the report ranks it a later visual reconstruction behind the primary texts. It draws the hull body and the 상장 as visibly separate structures, and the report says that may be the painter's convention and not the ship. Neither painting changes a number on this card. THE 문헌편 CLOSED, r210: the volume's remaining panokseon-bearing documents read whole at 113 dpi (pdf 7–12 and 123–127). 태종실록 태종 13년 2월 5일 (1413): the king, passing the 임진도 ferry, watches a 귀선 and a 왜선 fight a mock action. 태종 15년 7월 16일 (1415): 탁신's sixth point on the defences, 龜船之法 衝突衆敵 而敵不能害, with the order to build it sturdier and more skilfully. 선조실록 선조 25년 6월 21일 (1592): the 옥포–사천–당포–한산–안골포 campaign, the turtle ship first sent in at 사천 on 5월 29일 to fire its 총통 and burn the enemy ship. 당포파왜병장, 이순신's 1592 report: 別制龜船 前設龍頭 口放大砲 背植鐵尖 內能窺外 外不能窺內, the one contemporary description of the ship, and at 당포 倭船大如板屋者九隻 — nine Japanese ships as large as a panokseon, one carrying a 층루 three to four 장 high, under which the turtle ship's dragon mouth fired 현자 shot upward. 견내량파왜병장 and 조진수륙전사장: the turtle ship charges first and the panokseon follow (龜船先突 板屋次進), and a fleet of some 250 ships proposed by province. 난중일기 1592.2.27, 3.27 and 4.12: the turtle ship's gun trials. None of these documents carries a dimension of either ship. The one comparative size in the primary record is the 당포 sentence, the Japanese great ship as large as a panokseon. The name 귀선 is two centuries older than the panokseon: the 1413 and 1415 ship is a different vessel of the same name, and the report prints it first. THE 본문편 VII READ, r210 (pp. 210–214 and 227–232 at 113 dpi; the body-plan labels of pp. 111 and 213 confirmed at 300 dpi): the report's second design, the 전라좌수영 turtle ship. 표 28 (p. 212) repeats the 통제영's hull figures exactly — 전장 113, 본판장 64.8, 본판요광 14.5, 상요광 27 — and lowers the hull sides (선요고/현요고 8.0/7.5, 선두고 and 선미고 8.5, against 9.0/7.5 and 9.5/9.0) under a taller whole (전고 22.5 against 20.5). Its body plan (그림 196, p. 213) labels 27.8척 (상장광) over 27척 (상요광), and 표 29 (p. 230) prints 상장 요광 27.8척, 두광 20.4, 미광 13.8, with 13 crossbeams, 8 oars a side worked from a lowered 포판, 10 개판 ports and 6 bow ports a side. The 통제영's own table, 표 7 (p. 135), prints 상장 요광 33.8척, 두광 26.4, 미광 20.5, 15 crossbeams, 10 oars, 22 방패 ports and 12 doors a side, 12 개판 ports — 0.8척 over its body plan's 33. The crossbeams of both designs run past the 상장 edge: 가목 34.3척 under a 33.8척 deck (표 8, p. 136) and 28.6척 under 27.8 (표 30, p. 231). So one report sets the 상장 overhang at 3 to 3.4척 a side for the 통제영 ship and 0.4척 a side for the 좌수영 ship, on identical hull figures. The 통제영's 33 has the 1882 register behind it; the 좌수영's 27.8 has no register, only the 도설's sentence that the 좌수영 ship's dimensions were nearly the 통제영's. The Beam row now states both. With this read the research residual on this card is closed.

sekibune.hull.masts[0].top.provenance: RECORDED for the tradition, READ for the class. The wasen mast carried no top: the Minamichita wasen museum (minamichita-museum.com/wasen/ship.html) says the ropes on the yard, the boat and the anchor run through the semi, the sheave at the mast's upper end (帆柱上端の蝉（滑車）). The sekibune's own plate, the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593 (University of Tokyo; Commons File:Atakebune4.jpg, 2095 px across, about 16 px/m at the ships), draws one rigged mast in the fleet, the atakebune's: the yard slung at the head, about 17 px (about 1 m) of bare pole above it, stays running down from the head, and no platform. At that scale a block cannot be resolved. The semi is attested for the Edo wasen; on a sekibune of 1597 it is INFERRED from the tradition, and its form and size are derived from the pole (r327).
sekibune.hull.towerProvenance: The WALLED form is attested: the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593 (Univ. of Tokyo), this card's own plate, draws the yakata as a closed plank house with a ridged roof on hull after hull — the open pavilion drawn before round 117 was the class default (the panokseon's janggundae), not this plate. The PLAN is derived: no Sengoku sekibune survives, so the 4.5 x 2.8 m footprint, the 2.0 m eaves and the roof pitch are read off the scroll's hulls at ship scale — good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The scroll also hangs cloth in the wall openings of several cabins; since round 139 one opening a side is drawn with the cloth hung in it. The OPENING's size and place are derived — no cabin interior is attested, and the scroll resolves the openings only to ship scale — the cloth itself is the scroll's.
sekibune.hull.makuProvenance: The CLOTH is attested: the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593, this card's own plate, hangs a white band under a dark scalloped hem along the yagura band on hull after hull of the anchored fleet, and the atakebune amidships wears the same dress inverted — dark with white scallops — under sail. The scroll draws NO plank belt at this band, so gunDeck.walls (the panokseon's sangjang belt, round 118) is refuted for this class by its own plate. The DIMENSIONS are derived: the scroll stretches the upperworks, so the band's depth in metres cannot be read off it — the drawn cloth fills the band the model's own rail and deck bound, and the ~0.7 m scallop bay (makuBayM) is read off the scroll at its ~16 px/m (a ~25 m hull drawn ~400 px long), good to the nearest half metre, no finer. The BORDER's place and cut are the plate's own: on every hull that resolves it — the atakebune above all, the same dress at better scale — the scallops hang from the band's HEAD, tangent, cut from one strip, white cusps rising between them to the hanging line; until round 170 the drawn valance hung spaced discs off the band's FOOT, the record's own sentence inverted. The drawn valance is one strip a side, contiguous semicircles of half the recorded bay; its depth (a semicircle's, half the bay) is a class default — the scroll's stretch bars a finer read. Whether a sekibune cruised with the maku hung is not attested — the scroll's fleet is anchored, the atakebune wears hers under sail — and the ends of the band are left open: the plate shows the cloth only in broadside.
sekibune.hull.samaProvenance: The SLOTS are attested for the class: Japanese accounts of the sekibune have the so-yagura walled with tate-ita shield planks pierced by sama, firing slots for bow and arquebus — the wall's purpose on a hull that mounts no broadside. The COUNT, SIZE and HEIGHT are derived: no Sengoku sekibune survives, and the Busan scroll (~16 px/m) resolves the yagura band but not individual slots, so 13 a side is set from the oar-station rhythm the length itself is derived from, and each slot is drawn 0.10 m wide by 0.36 m tall, centred 0.90 m over the fighting deck — the height a man standing on that deck fires from. Since round 140 the slots are OPENINGS cut through the drawn plank, with reveal faces the plank's own thickness deep and a dark board behind each so the slot reads into the deck's shadow; before that each was a dark plate laid on the wall's face.
sekibune.hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r176 — the windlass question for this hull, opened by the r172 residual, closes with nothing drawn, and this field says why. Her tradition's machine is the rokuro, and it is not a windlass: the surviving spindle and the Hokyu-maru model at the Minamichita wasen museum (photographs read this round, form only, no scale on the pages) show a vertical tapered spindle standing between a lower deck and an overhead beam, two long bars passed through it crosswise at different heights, the rope winding at its foot. Both fetched descriptions place and rig it the same way: two sets inside the aft yagura house, the line from the masthead semi block over the stern tobi-guruma block, winding yard, tender and anchor from within the ship (Minamichita wasen museum; Museum of Maritime Science monoshiri sheet 28). Every attestation is the Edo cargo tradition — the bezaisen, a type that postdates this drawn ship — and the museum's own sentence treats the machine's installation aboard as a development within that tradition. No fetched source puts a rokuro, or any winch, on a sekibune or any Sengoku warship; the Murakami Suigun Museum states the sekibune and kobaya barely appear in contemporary documents or drawings at all. Drawing one would stack three unsourced inferences: era (1597 against Edo attestations), class (cargo to war, with no textual bridge like the Tiangong Kaiwu's statement that the ocean transport's gear was all the same), and placement (the attested stand is inside an aft working house between floor and beam; this ship's aft house is the commander's yakata). The record stays silent and the builder draws nothing. That her hands hoisted by direct pull is itself an inference, marked as one on the card. Scope: this judgment is for the drawn 1597 instance; the class ran to 1868, an Edo sekibune shares the attested machine's own era, and a drawn Edo instance would reopen the question.
sekibune.hull.anchorProvenance: The PRESENCE and the FORM are the plate's and the era's. The card's own plate — the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593, Univ. of Tokyo — draws the anchored fleet riding to twisted cables and, at the barrier line's upper and lower ends, the anchor itself at the cable's end: stockless, short-shanked, four strongly recurved claws (crops read r187; the lower one is clipped at the sheet edge). The era and class evidence agrees and points at her: on Ishii Kenji's evidence (1983, via Matsui Hironobu, Kanazawa Univ. archaeology bulletin 34, 2013, the four-claw iron anchor's typological study) — the anchor drawn in the 1433 Jingu Kogo engi emaki, and the 1486 Boshi nyuminki recording iron anchors on the Ming embassy ships — warships and special ships carried the four-claw iron anchor alongside wood-stone anchors from the first half of the 15th century, while wood and stone stayed the ordinary wasen's mainstay until the mid-17th: an early-1600s Osaka screen counts one iron anchor to eight wood-stone. The NAME and the making are the wasen tradition's: the Minamichita wasen museum's sentence — a square iron bar, its tip split in four and the quarters bent outward into claws, the count varying with the ship's size — and the Tomo anchor-smiths' recorded process (Tamura 1978, via Matsui). Every DIMENSION is a named default: no sekibune anchor survives. The drawn 2.0 m overall sits inside Matsui's measured corpus of 49 survivors (1.05–3.03 m, nearly all Edo–Meiji), at the corpus's own small/large break — about 120 kg by the Kozushima seabed anchor's calibration (2.8 m raised at 330–340 kg), a direct-pull load for a crew whose rokuro is judged silent (r176); ring and arm proportions follow the corpus and Matsui's fig. 1. The plate is at ship scale (~16 px/m) and no dimension is taken from it. COUNT is not recorded: one is drawn; Ishii's sentence has iron used alongside wood-stone on the warships, and that mixed tackle is not drawn — no count or mix is attested for her class. The STOW is a placement inference, the fleet rule (r182–r186): recovered on the open foredeck forward of the so-yagura — the bow is where the tradition works its anchor: the Edo bezaisen rests it on the uwakannuki, a hard-oak member on the bow's topmost rail, and belays the cable there (Minamichita, the same page; that beam is Edo cargo structure and is not drawn) — rolled 45 degrees, pitched to the deck's own gradient, settled by measured box; the cable bent to the free accessory ring and flaked in a coil beside it — no belay is attested and she has no winding machine. A measured Sengoku warship anchor, or the 1433 emaki plate in resolution, replaces the defaults and this field says so. Member sections are the corpus's own record, read r191: 表1 of the same paper (Matsui 2013 p.38) measures all 49 anchors at member level, and the arms are RECTANGULAR forged bars — 最大幅×最大厚 at the root, a wide thin blade at the fluke tip. Corpus means for the 27 consistently-printed anchors ≥190 cm, as fractions of 全長: root 0.0346±0.0037 × 0.0198±0.0033, tip 0.0220±0.0052 × 0.0058±0.0031. Both rings take the type anchor the class already cites (Onominato a: teardrop 44×19 cm of 3 cm bar, accessory ring ⌀36 of 4×4.5 section, on 269 cm). The weight field kg 122 is DERIVED by cube-law from the corpus's one weighed anchor — the Kozushima wreck anchor, 2.8 m, 330–340 kg by forklift (約90貫), raised 1990 — 15.26 kg per m³ of 全長³. The shank's two stations are the Pacific corpus's own calipers, read r192: 表3 of 二宮俊洋's master's survey (東京海洋大学 2014, oacis record 1018 — 144 anchors, Ibaraki to Wakayama, the companion survey to Matsui's) records the shank per anchor at the clean upper bar (軸正面×軸側面) and at the root boss where the four arms are forged on (軸根本正面×軸根本側面). Corpus means as fractions of 全長, each anchor's pair sorted (min,max) because the shrine's mounting sets which face is 正面: upper bar 0.0214±0.0046 × 0.0303±0.0058 (n=17), root boss 0.0491±0.0072 × 0.0764±0.0099 (n=16); excluded by name №1 (sea-concreted, every member ~2× corpus), №74 (exfoliated to 0.012 of 全長) and №93 (printed-inconsistent, a 0.36·全長 root), and №82's shaft pair flagged (側面/正面 = 2.8, twice anyone else) and dropped. The r191 CONTEST is RESOLVED, in the record's favour on both sides: the monument photographs' 0.023–0.034 was the upper bar, and the old solve's 0.047 was the root boss (0.0491) — the real shank tapers hard from an oblong boss to a slender near-square bar, and both prior readings were right at their own stations. The drawn shank now carries exactly those stations; the knee where the taper meets the bar is the one dimension no table records, SOLVED so the drawn iron weighs the record's kg at 7850 kg/m³ — at (2.0 m, 122 kg) it lands at 77% of the shank, inside the drawn form's own solvable band (69–138 kg); a record outside that band would clamp the knee and the mass audit would convict, a contest and not a knob. Cross-corpus check on the members already held: №71 (銚子, 300 cm) calipers claw root 0.0350×0.0233 and claw length 0.320 of 全長 against Matsui's 0.0346×0.0198 and the drawn 0.30 — two independent coasts agree on the arms. Residual: the mass calibration still hangs on the Kozushima weighing alone (約90貫 by forklift); the 1993 site report (東京都教育委員会, per the nabunken bibliography — print only, not surfaced open) would firm the kg, no longer the shank. The audit holds the drawn iron to the record's weight (V-YMASS, 12%) and the drawn shank's end sections to the calipered stations (V-YSHANK, 12%).

fluyt.hull.rakeProvenance: AUTHORED to fill the record's own allowance: loa 32.0 − lwl 27.5 leaves 4.5 m of overhang and the drawn planking carried only 3.84 m of it (rakes 0.07/0.05, r137 sweep −0.66). Generated type record, so both figures are class figures, not one ship's. The authored 7:5 stem:stern split is kept and normalized up to the allowance: 0.0820/0.0586, drawn 2.62 m bow / 1.88 m stern, 32.00 m to the centimetre. The fluyt profile — rounded stem falling forward, narrow tuck with the poop overhanging aft (Witsen via Hoving, 17th-century Dutch shipbuilding practice) — supports bow > stern qualitatively, not to the centimetre.
fluyt.hull.headProvenance: Type-period CLASS DEFAULT, no hull-specific plate: the Dutch fluyt of c. 1620 carried a beakhead under the bowsprit, a knee of the head with one headrail a side (Witsen 1671; the van de Velde drawings); grade 1, the single rail.
fluyt.hull.masts[0].courseAtProvenance: PLATE READ, r330 (0y¹⁷⁴): the fore course yard hangs at 0.879 of the height from the deck to the fore top, read off Wenceslaus Hollar, 'Navis Mercatoria Hollandica, vulgo VLIET', etching, 1647 (Wikimedia Commons File:Wenceslas Hollar - A Flute (State 2).jpg, read at the 1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r328/dl/hollar-flute.jpg, about 36 px/m at the masts, bow at the left). The deck at this mast is row 902, the foot of the forecastle rail's lattice, where the mast stands on the forecastle deck (r329's deck for this mast). The top is row 563, the upper edge of the top. The top shows as a dark band on rows 563-572 at columns 740-758, aft of the topsail's leech, with the topmast shrouds' deadeyes above it, drawn as the main top is drawn. Its fore half is behind the topsail. The course yard was traced from column 660 to 772 (29 points, a straight line within 1.6 px rms), and it crosses the mast's axis at row 604. The axis there is taken at column 708, on the line from the mast's foot (column 724, row 902) to the topmast's cap (column 693, row 285); 8 px of error in that column moves the crossing by 1.6 px. The yard is drawn sloping, its after yardarm higher, because it is braced round and the ship is seen from a little forward of the beam; the model hangs it level at the crossing. The deck-to-top span is 339 px, so a 3 px reading error is 0.009 of it, and the bound is 0.03. Until r330 this course hung at the class 0.60 of the lower mast, 0.667 of the deck-to-top height, which no plate set. The hull is dated 1620 and the plate 1647.
fluyt.hull.masts[0].mastHeightsProvenance: READ, r329 (0y¹⁷¹), the top re-read r330 (0y¹⁷⁴): the top 9.39 m, the topmast's head 17.1 m and the head of the pole above it (built as the topgallant mast) 20.53 m over the foot of the mast. Each is a share of the distance between the fore and mizzen masts' feet (0.4363, 0.7941, 0.9537), times that distance on this hull's built masts (21.53 m). Read off Wenceslaus Hollar, 'Navis Mercatoria Hollandica, vulgo VLIET', etching, 1647 (Wikimedia Commons File:Wenceslas Hollar - A Flute (State 2).jpg, read at the 1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r328/dl/hollar-flute.jpg, about 36 px/m at the masts, bow at the left): the fore and mizzen masts meet the deck at columns 724 and 1501, 777 px apart; the deck at this mast is taken at the foot of the forecastle rail's lattice, where the mast stands on the forecastle deck (row 902, to about 8 px); the top's upper edge is on row 563 (r329 read the top on row 600; that is the row where the course yard crosses the mast's column 724, and the top stands 37 px above it, a band on rows 563-572 aft of the topsail with the topmast shrouds' deadeyes above it, drawn as the main top is; from r329 to r330 the fore top stood 1.02 m too low), the topmast's head, where its shrouds meet under the cap, on row 285, and the head of the pole above it on row 161. Under sail Hollar draws that pole bare, with a pennant on it and no yard crossed; his second fluyt plate of 1647 (the fluyts at anchor, 'vulgo VLIETEN', build/staging/r328/dl/fleuten-1647.jpg, 644 px wide) draws topgallant masts with yards crossed on the fore and the main. So the pole is built as the topgallant mast, and the three tiers stand. The tops and caps are read to about 5 px, 0.006 of the span. The datum is the masts' feet, as on the East Indiaman and the slave ship (r322). CONTESTED datum: Hollar draws the ship a little from forward of the beam, so the horizontal span is foreshortened and these heights may be a few per cent high. Until r329 the mast was Steel's 1794 proportions (lower mast a share of Steel's main, topmast 0.60, topgallant 0.50), a rule for warships 150 years later; the lower tops stood 4.4 to 5.7 m higher. The hull is dated 1620 and the plate 1647. Until r333 the hull's stations put the main 0.606 of the way from the fore to the mizzen, where the plate draws it at 0.539; since r333 it stands at the plate's share (masts[1].atProvenance).
fluyt.hull.masts[0].hoistProvenance: PLATE READ, r331 (0y¹⁷⁶): the fore topsail yard, read off Wenceslaus Hollar, 'Navis Mercatoria Hollandica, vulgo VLIET', etching, 1647 (Wikimedia Commons File:Wenceslas Hollar - A Flute (State 2).jpg, read at the 1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r328/dl/hollar-flute.jpg, about 36 px/m at the masts, bow at the left). The head of the topmast is row 285, the topmast's cap, where the ring of the crosstrees shows at column 693. The yard stands 0.9115 of the height from the foot to the topmast's head. fluyt.hull.masts[0].topmastTopProvenance: UNREAD, r325 (0y¹⁶⁷): the topmast carries crosstrees at its head, the class fitting, and no plate of this hull's topmasts has been read for a top. east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].courseAtProvenance: PLATE READ, r320 (0y¹⁵⁷): the crossjack hangs at 0.848 of the height from the deck to the mizzen top, read off Hocker, F. (ed.), Vasa II: Rigging and Sailing a Swedish Warship of 1628 (Vasamuseet / Nordic Academic Press, 2023), p. 31, the rig diagram, as Wikimedia Commons File:Vasa_rig_diagram.jpg (1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r320/dl/vasa-rig.jpg) on the mizzen's own column: the mast meets the hull at row 944, the top is centred on row 700 (its platform 697-703) and the crossjack crosses the mast at rows 736-738. The deck-to-top span is 244 px, so a 3 px reading error is 0.012 of it. The drawing gives the hull as a silhouette and draws no deck under the poop rail, so both deck datums are the row where the mast meets the hull; a rail of 1 m would raise the share by about 0.014, and the bound is 0.03. Mainwaring's Seaman's Dictionary (c. 1620-23, NRS vol. 56 p. 135) agrees: "Cross-jack is a yard at the upper end of the mizen mast under the top ... the use whereof is to spread and haul on the mizen-topsail sheets". This hull is dated 1620; the read is Vasa's, applied to it.
east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].crossjackProvenance: CLASS, r315 (0y¹⁴⁹): the crossjack is crossed bare, with no sail set from it and none rolled on it. No plate of this hull's mizzen has been read. Class source: Falconer, An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (1769), CROSS-JACK: 'a sail extended on the lower yard of the mizen-mast, which is hence called the cross-jack yard ... This sail, however, has generally been found of little service, and is therefore very seldom used.' The Asow plate (Eckersberg 1828) shows a 74's crossjack bare at anchor; this hull takes the same rule unread.
east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].mizzenSailProvenance: CLASS, r317 (0y¹⁵²): the mizzen sets a lateen under its topsail, from a yard slung to the lower mast. This hull is dated 1620; no plate of its mizzen has been read. Class source: Waters, D. W., The Art of Navigation in England in Elizabethan and Early Stuart Times (London, 1958), ch. I: 'The larger vessels were square-rigged only, or "cross-sailed" as it was termed, with three masts and a bowsprit. The fore and main masts each carried a course and a top-sail, the bow-sprit a sprit-sail; all these were "cross-sails"; the mizzen mast carried a lateen-sail. This rig remained typical of merchant ships well into the eighteenth' century (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.51856, full text). Falconer 1769, MIZEN, still describes the mizzen as 'extended sometimes by a gaff, and sometimes by a yard which crosses the mast obliquely'. The yard's length, angle and heel are read off Vasa's rig diagram (lateenYardProvenance, r321).
east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].tiersProvenance: PLATE READ, r320 (0y¹⁵⁷): the mizzen crosses two square yards, the crossjack under the top and the topsail on the topmast, and no topgallant. Hocker, F. (ed.), Vasa II: Rigging and Sailing a Swedish Warship of 1628 (Vasamuseet / Nordic Academic Press, 2023), p. 31, the rig diagram, as Wikimedia Commons File:Vasa_rig_diagram.jpg (1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r320/dl/vasa-rig.jpg) names the masts and spars of a 1628 ship: "(i) mizzenmast; (j) mizzen topmast", and the sails "(9) mizzen; (10) mizzen topsail". Fore and main each carry a topgallant mast, (e) and (h); the mizzen has none. This hull is dated 1620 and has no plate of its own; Vasa is the nearest ship of the period whose rig is recovered, and the rule is read from her.
east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].lateenYardProvenance: PLATE READ, r321 (0y¹⁵⁸): the mizzen lateen yard lies at 42.1° from the horizontal, is 1.576 times the horizontal distance between the main and mizzen masts' feet, and has its heel on the deck 0.531 of that distance before the mizzen, so its peak stands over the taffrail. Read off Hocker, F. (ed.), Vasa II: Rigging and Sailing a Swedish Warship of 1628 (Vasamuseet / Nordic Academic Press, 2023), p. 31, the rig diagram, as Wikimedia Commons File:Vasa_rig_diagram.jpg (1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r320/dl/vasa-rig.jpg, about 24 px/m on Vasa's 61 m hull): the yard's brown line was fitted on 346 columns (slope 0.904, rms 1.3 px); its peak is at column 112 row 599, where the spar tapers to a grey hairline over the taffrail (column 88), and its heel at column 500 row 950 on the hull's upper edge. The mizzen's axis meets the hull at column 323.7 row 944 and the main's at column 655.6 row 1012, 331.9 px apart; the yard is 523 px. A 5 px error at the faint peak is 0.015 of the spacing, and the bound on each share is 0.03 and on the angle 1°. On Vasa the yard crosses the mizzen at 0.717 of the height from the deck to the mizzen top. The yard is keyed to the masts' stations and not to the mizzen's height: in r321 this hull's masts were still Steel's 1794 proportions, and keying the yard to that mizzen drew a 44 m yard on a 45 m hull. Since r322 the mizzen takes Vasa's heights too (mastHeightsProvenance), and the yard crosses it at 0.743 of the height from the deck to the top, 0.026 above Vasa's 0.717. The clew is still the class 0.62 of the yard abaft the tack. This hull is dated 1620 and has no plate of its own; the read is Vasa's, applied to it.
east-indiaman.hull.masts[2].mastHeightsProvenance: READ, r322 (0y¹⁶⁴): the top 9.98 m and the topmast's head (cap) 19.83 m over the foot of the mast. These are Vasa's mizzen heights as shares of the distance between her fore and mizzen masts' feet (0.2954, 0.5872), times that distance on this hull's built masts (33.774 m). Read off Hocker, F. (ed.), Vasa II: Rigging and Sailing a Swedish Warship of 1628 (Vasamuseet / Nordic Academic Press, 2023), p. 31, the rig diagram, as Wikimedia Commons File:Vasa_rig_diagram.jpg (1920 px thumbnail, build/staging/r320/dl/vasa-rig.jpg, about 24 px/m on Vasa's hull): the fore and mizzen masts meet the hull at columns 1149.6 and 323.7, 825.9 px apart; this mast meets it at row 944; the top platform is centred on row 700, the cap of the topmast's head on row 459. Above the cap Vasa's mizzen carries a bare staff to row 366 (0.6998); no sail is set on it and it is not built (the mast is built in two pieces, `only` 2). Each row is read to 3 px, which is 0.004 of the span. The heights are keyed to the masts' feet, the same datum as the mizzen lateen yard (r321), because the stations are a hull datum the builder carries. CONTESTED datum: keyed to the hull's length overall instead (taffrail to beakhead, 1447 px on the plate), the heights come out 0.86-0.88 of these. Until r322 the mast was Steel's 1794 proportions (lower mast a share of Steel's main, topmast 0.60, topgallant 0.50), a rule for warships 170 years later. This hull is dated 1620 and has no plate of its own; the read is Vasa's (1628), applied to it.

east-indiaman.hull.sternLightProvenance: CLASS DEFAULTS, not a read of this hull: the small-pane grid is the period's glazing technology — crown glass casts no metre pane — and the one plate in hand is English (SLR0338, see ship-of-the-line). Dutch retourschip practice ran leaded lights with smaller panes if anything, so 3×3 is a floor, not a count of this stern; pier share and pitch are carried from the same plate as class figures.
east-indiaman.hull.capstanProvenance: Bar capstan of the European tradition, a type-period CLASS DEFAULT — no hull-specific plate; counts are class defaults (whelps 6: Falconer 1769 pl. II figs 11-12 resolve six, period range 6-8). Form and proportions from Falconer 1769 CAPSTERN (whelps drumhead-to-deck like buttresses, chocks, two iron pawls, bars heaved at the breast) and pl. II fig 11 (engraving, widths ~±10%: height ≈ 0.86 of drumhead dia, neck sweep 0.82 flaring to 1.0 at the deck). Sized to the men at its bars.

ship-of-the-line.hull.masts[2].furlStowProvenance: READ, r312 (0y¹³⁸): BRAILED. This hull is a class 74 with no single ship behind it, so the plate is the nearest dated painting of a working 74 at anchor by a painter known for drawing rigging exactly: C. W. Eckersberg, 'The Russian Ship of the Line Asow and a Frigate at Anchor in the Roads of Elsinore', 1828, oil on canvas, Statens Museum for Kunst (Commons 'C.W. Eckersberg - The Russian Ship of the Line "Asow" and a Frigate at Anchor in the Roads of Elsinore - Google Art Project.jpg', 4044 x 4939 px, read off the 1920 px derivative; build/staging/r312/plates/asow.jpg, the mizzen at 2x in asow-mizzen-2x.png and at 3x in asow-mizzen-3x.png). Asow (Azov) was a Russian 74 launched in 1826 (Commons 'Category:Azov (ship, 1826)'); the painting shows her at anchor with her yards crossed and every square sail furled, seen from high on her starboard quarter. At the mizzen it is about 20 px/m on the 1920 px derivative: about 410 px from the poop rail to the mizzen top. A gaff 0.25 m thick would show 5 px wide. WHAT IT SHOWS: a long buff bundle of canvas lies close along the after side of the mizzen lower mast, from just under the crossjack yard down to the poop, where the boom lies fore and aft over the taffrail; the St Andrew's ensign hangs from the peak of a gaff that stands aloft. That is the spanker brailed in to the mast under a standing gaff, with the boom left in place. CONTESTED: this is one painting of one ship, a Russian 74 forty-eight years after this hull's 1780, and a painting, not a photograph. The ensign hides the gaff's own line, so its angle is not read, and the gaff's length and the boom's height are not read either. The builder's 'lowered' default (a schooner's stowage) is not shown on any plate of a 74 that has been read.
ship-of-the-line.hull.masts[2].courseAtProvenance: PLATE READ, r313 (0y¹⁴³): the crossjack hangs at 0.845 of the height from the deck to the mizzen top (bound +/-0.025). Plate: C. W. Eckersberg, 'The Russian Ship of the Line Asow and a Frigate at Anchor in the Roads of Elsinore', 1828 (Commons, Google Art Project copy, read off the 1920 px derivative, build/staging/r312/plates/asow.jpg; the mizzen lower rig at about 30 px/m, from the main yard's length). She is seen from abaft her starboard quarter with the eye near the water, so the masts stand upright on the canvas and heights along one mast keep their ratios. Rows on the derivative, read as brightness profiles in columns 330-370 and 600-640, either side of the mizzen and clear of the ensign: the crossjack, a pale yard, rows 1430-1449, centre 1438; the main yard, dark, crosses just above it at 1416-1428; the front edge of the mizzen top 1372 (+/-6); the mizzen cap 1283; the taffrail's top at the mast 1782. The poop deck at the mast is hidden behind the taffrail, so its row lies between 1782 and about 1815 (a 1 m rail at 30 px/m); the two datums give 0.839 and 0.851, and the record takes their mean. The builder stands the top's centre at 0.90 of the lower mast, so the crossjack hangs at 0.845 x 0.90 of the lower mast; the class figure it replaces was 0.60 of the lower mast, which put the yard at 0.665 of the deck-to-top height. CONTESTED: one painting of one ship, a Russian 74 launched in 1826, 46 years after this hull's 1780. The plate also shows the mizzen's proportions differ from the model's: its masthead, cap to top, is 0.18 of the deck-to-cap height and the model's is 0.12, so the read is taken against the top, where the yard's slings hang, and not against the cap.
ship-of-the-line.hull.masts[2].crossjackProvenance: PLATE READ, r315 (0y¹⁴⁹): the crossjack is crossed bare, with no sail set from it and none rolled on it. Plate: C. W. Eckersberg, 'The Russian Ship of the Line Asow and a Frigate at Anchor in the Roads of Elsinore', 1828 (Commons, Google Art Project copy, read off the 1920 px derivative, about 30 px/m at the mizzen, the eye near the water): the crossjack is a pale spar, rows 1430-1449, lit on its upper face, with no roll on it, while every other yard on the three masts carries its furled sail. Class source in agreement: Falconer, An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (1769), CROSS-JACK: 'a sail extended on the lower yard of the mizen-mast, which is hence called the cross-jack yard ... This sail, however, has generally been found of little service, and is therefore very seldom used.' Contested: the plate shows her at anchor; it cannot show whether she ever set a crossjack at sea, and Falconer says it was very seldom done.
ship-of-the-line.hull.masts[2].hoistProvenance: UNREAD, r324 (0y¹⁶⁶): each yard above the course is set atrip, at 0.88 of the section it hoists on, the class figure (Falconer 1769, ATRIP: 'The top-sails are said to be atrip, when they are hoisted up to the top-mast-heads'), and no plate of this hull's set sails has been read for it.
ship-of-the-line.hull.sternLightProvenance: The tier arrangement is a PLATE READ: SLR0338, the RMG contemporary full-hull model of Bellona (1760), a Slade 74 — the record's own sub-type. Astern photograph (RMG media c1099, 1041×1280) at ~55 px/m: five pilaster pitches span 335 px and the ~9.2 m stern flat ~510 px, so pane COUNTS are solid and widths good to ~±15%, no finer. Each light in BOTH tiers is a 3×3 pane grid — two vertical and two horizontal bars, the 2–4 px bright lines a column-brightness profile finds inside every light; glazing fills 74–80% of pitch (pier assembly 17 px of 66–71) at 1.20–1.29 m pitch. The colour quarter plate (RMG media d7827) resolves the mica panes recessed BEHIND the gilt bars. Until round 171 each drawn light was one uncastable 0.9 m sheet with a single stick, floating proud of its own frame, and 36% of the tier was blank wall.
ship-of-the-line.hull.capstanProvenance: PLATE READS off RMG SLR0338, the contemporary Bellona model, quarter plate l5785_003 (~16 px/m at the waist — counts solid ±1, widths ±15%): bars SHIPPED, 12-14 rays so bars=14 is a read ±1; drumhead ≈1.5 m (read at that px/m, ±10%); bar tips ≈2.7 drumhead-dias out, agreeing with the period's 12-14 ft bars; the machine painted red-ochre like the inner works (paint field). whelps 6 is a CLASS DEFAULT (Falconer pl. II resolves six; period range 6-8). Form per Falconer 1769 CAPSTERN: whelps drumhead-to-deck, chocks between, two iron pawls on deck, men heaving breast-high. A 74 carried main (double) and jeer capstans; the weather-deck machine drawn is the upper barrel of the main.

slave-ship.hull.masts[2].mizzenSailProvenance: CLASS, r317 (0y¹⁵²): the mizzen sets a lateen under its topsail, from a yard slung to the lower mast. The fore and main masts each carried a course and a top-sail, the bow-sprit a sprit-sail; all these were "cross-sails"; the mizzen mast carried a lateen-sail. slave-ship.hull.rakeProvenance: AUTHORED to fill the record's own allowance: loa 30.0 − lwl 26.0 leaves 4.0 m of overhang and the drawn planking carried only 1.5 m of it (rakes 0.03/0.02, r129 fleet sweep). preussen.hull.masts[0].yardsProvenance: RECORD: six yards on each of her five masts - course, lower and upper topsail, lower and upper topgallant, royal - the five-masted full-rigged ship's thirty square sails as Tecklenborg rigged her in 1902; the record's own attested spar lengths (the 32 m course yard, the 16 m royal yard) are in mastProvenance. No plate was re-read for the count in r282.
preussen.hull.masts[0].reefs.provenance: UNREAD, r284: no plate of this ship's square sails has been read for reef bands; every tier is drawn plain, which is the silence named, not a read. A plate of any tier's face at 50 px/m or better would settle which tiers carry bands and at what row.
preussen.hull.masts[0].yardFracsProvenance: PLATE READ, r289, on the r286 read: the State Library of Victoria's Brodie collection print of Preussen at anchor, 'PREUSSEN. Only ship ever rigged like this.' (Malcolm Brodie shipping collection, accession H99.220/3712, gelatin silver 9.5 x 15.5 cm, between 1902 and 1910, catalogue alma9917506533607636, Rosetta IE40684, master FL15666487.tif 5421x4071 served as the JPG derivative FL21230608; out of copyright; build/staging/r289/full-IE40684.jpg, the whole plate at half scale with a 200 px grid in plate-IE40684-half-grid.png, each mast in crop-anchor-*.png, the trucks at 4x in sheet-anchor-trucks-4x.png, the rails at 2x in sheet-anchor-rails-2x.png). She lies square on the starboard beam, bow to the left, the whole hull and every truck in the frame at one scale: the mast spacing 796 / 796 / 770 / 702 px against the record's stations (0.18 / 0.18 / 0.18 / 0.16 of L, which at one scale is 796 / 796 / 796 / 708), so no foreshortening is measurable; 30.6 px/m from the main mast's attested 58 m. The upper topsail, upper topgallant and royal yards are LOWERED onto their doublings, so only the three FIXED yards - course, lower topsail, lower topgallant - and the trucks are read here; the three hoisting yards keep r286's figures (0.54 / 0.80 / 0.92), which this plate cannot read. METHOD as r286: each mast's centreline fitted through the pole (sd 2.5-3.4 px); a yard read as the dark bar crossing bands 60-220 px out on both sides, the crossing row the mean of the two sides; the truck the top of the pole's dark run, read on 4x crops (+/- 5 px); the DECK the top of the dark topsides on the mast's forward side (the cap rail, +/- 8 px) plus the r215 class bulwark depth of 1.35 m (41 px, +/- 0.3 m) - the plate's painted-ports band stands only on the midship island, and there its lower edge (2843) agrees with the neighbouring masts' rail + 41 (2841, 2833), which is the datum's check. ROWS: fore truck 1108, rail 2775, deck 2815, lower topgallant 1644.5, lower topsail 2127, course 2381.5 (the lowered upper topsail 2070, the lowered upper topgallant 1600); main truck 1068, rail 2800, deck 2841, lower topgallant 1625, lower topsail 2107, course 2359.5 (the lowered upper topsail 2048, the lowered upper topgallant 1577); kreuz truck 1098, the midship island's rail 2750 and its painted-ports band 2813-2843, deck 2843 (the band's foot), lower topgallant 1655, lower topsail 2132.5, course 2390 (the lowered upper topsail 2069, the lowered upper topgallant 1606); laeisz truck 1210, rail 2795, deck 2833, lower topgallant 1743.5, lower topsail 2219.5, course 2473.5 (the lowered upper topsail 2164, the lowered upper topgallant 1703); jigger truck 1408, rail 2800, deck 2833, lower topgallant 1868, lower topsail 2287, course 2511.5 (the lowered upper topsail 2229, the lowered upper topgallant 1825). FRACTIONS OF THE TRUCK OVER THE DECK, per mast: fore course 0.254, lower topsail 0.403, lower topgallant 0.686; deck to truck 1707 px, 55.8 m; main course 0.272, lower topsail 0.414, lower topgallant 0.686; deck to truck 1773 px, 58.0 m (the scale's anchor); kreuz course 0.260, lower topsail 0.407, lower topgallant 0.681; deck to truck 1745 px, 57.1 m; laeisz course 0.221, lower topsail 0.378, lower topgallant 0.671; deck to truck 1623 px, 53.1 m; jigger course 0.226, lower topsail 0.383, lower topgallant 0.677; deck to truck 1425 px, 46.6 m. RECORDED PER MAST, to 0.01, because the plate reads the same split r286 could not resolve - the two after masts hang their three lower yards lower than the three forward masts by 0.03-0.04 of their trucks - and reads it square on the beam with every mast at one scale: fore 0.25 / 0.40 / 0.69, main 0.27 / 0.41 / 0.69, kreuz 0.26 / 0.41 / 0.68, laeisz 0.22 / 0.38 / 0.67, jigger 0.23 / 0.38 / 0.68. AGAINST r286 (the Green plate from the quarter, per mast): the course within 0.025 (jigger 0.20 -> 0.23, laeisz 0.21 -> 0.22, kreuz 0.25 -> 0.26, main 0.27 -> 0.27), the lower topsail within 0.03, the lower topgallant within 0.01; r286's +/- 0.04 on the two lowest yards was that split, and it is real. BOUNDS: +/- 0.01 on every fraction (the truck +/- 5, the deck +/- 10 and the yard +/- 4 px on 1425-1773 px of truck over deck; the bulwark's +/- 0.3 m moves a fraction by under 0.005). THE TRUCKS: deck to truck reads 1707 / 1773 / 1745 / 1623 / 1425 px on the five masts at one scale, so the after masts are SHORTER - the main's attested 58 m is the tallest, and the fore is 55.8, the kreuz 57.1, the laeisz 53.1 and the jigger 46.6 m (+/- 0.5 m; the datum's uncertainty moves all five alike and the ratios to the main hold); r286's Green plate had the jigger's truck-over-deck 2256 px against the laeisz's 2310 although the jigger stood nearer that camera, the same finding unread. NOT READ HERE: the spar lengths (the yards' dark runs are broken by the lowered yards and the rigging; courseYardM 32 stands attested); the bulwark's own height (assumed at the class 1.35 m); the three hoisting yards' set heights. THIS MAST (fore, station 0.16): rows truck 1108, rail 2775, deck 2815, lower topgallant 1644.5, lower topsail 2127, course 2381.5 (the lowered upper topsail 2070, the lowered upper topgallant 1600); read course 0.254, lower topsail 0.403, lower topgallant 0.686; deck to truck 1707 px, 55.8 m. PLATE READ, r290, the three HOISTING yards: the State Library of Victoria's halftone of Preussen under full sail from aft of the port beam - r289's census called it square on the beam at 22 px/m off the 1200 px preview, and it is oblique, 37-49 px/m across the hull, as this paragraph measures below; corrected r291 (Malcolm Brodie shipping collection, accession H99.220/4261, 'A mass of canvas to attend to in a ship like this', Rosetta IE32693, 5421 x 4071, the JPG derivative at the master's width by the r289 route; out of copyright; build/staging/r290/full-IE32693.jpg, the whole plate at half scale with a 200 px grid in ../r289/plate-IE32693-half-grid.png, each mast in crop-marked-*.png with its fitted line and the yard rows drawn, the mastheads at 2x in sheet-trucks-2x.png, the hull's band at 2x in sheet-band-2x.png, the main's band profiles in profile-main.png). Bow to the RIGHT, the camera a little aft of the beam (the mast spacing 890 / 900 / 780 / 700 px jigger to fore, so the forward masts are farther and smaller), all six yards SET on every mast, the halftone cell about 8 px. METHOD (read-fullsail.py, read-fullsail3.py, read-register.py): each pole found by a line search over its sky rows on a 4 px blurred plate (mean brightness along the line, slope 0.03-0.09 px/row); bands 60-220 px out on both sides profiled per row on the unblurred plate; under full sail a yard is the HEAD of its sail and the canvas is darkest just under it, so a yard is the sharp light-to-dark edge going down the plate on both sides (the steepest 24-row descent; the two sides averaged; six on every mast). THE DATUM IS REGISTERED, NOT READ: this plate's trucks are hidden by cloud (kreuz) or faint against bright sky (fore), and the painted-ports band's foot at the deck is overlaid by the forecastle and the boats forward, so the plate's own truck and deck reads disagreed with r289's fixed yards by up to 0.12 at the fore; instead each mast's deck row D and truck-over-deck T were solved by least squares from its course, lower topsail and lower topgallant rows against r289's per-mast fractions (three rows, two unknowns; residuals under 4 px on four masts and 7 px on the fore), and the three hoisting yards read as fractions in that frame. READ PER MAST (utop / utg / royal): fore upper topsail 0.558, upper topgallant 0.820, royal 0.942; main upper topsail 0.561, upper topgallant 0.809, royal 0.923; kreuz upper topsail 0.557, upper topgallant 0.805, royal 0.919; laeisz upper topsail 0.538, upper topgallant 0.799, royal 0.936; jigger upper topsail 0.550, upper topgallant 0.813, royal 0.923. BOUND +/- 0.02 on each (the edge row +/- 8 px on 2050-2435 px of T, and the registration's own +/- 0.01 per fixed yard propagated through T).
