preussen.hull.masts[4].furlStowProvenance: UNREAD, r310: no plate of this hull furled has been read for how this sail is stowed. The builder lowers the gaff onto a roll along the boom, a schooner's stowage; that is the default named, not a read. A plate of her at anchor that shows this mast between the deck and the top settles it: a gaff standing at its working angle with the sail gathered against the mast is 'brailed'; no gaff aloft is 'lowered'.
preussen.hull.deck.provenance: SOLID BULWARK, r291: hull.freeboard 5.0 is the SKIN's top, the cap rail over the water (the r215 semantics; the 5.0 itself carries no provenance and stands as the class set it), and the deck lies 1.35 m under it (deck.belowSheerM), so the five masts, whose truckM figures are attested and read deck-to-truck, stand on the deck and not on the cap. Before r291 the deck was drawn at the skin's top: every mast heel, every yard and the card's 58 m deck-to-truck were measured from the cap rail, 1.35 m higher over the water than the reads that placed them. THE DEPTH is the r215 class figure, which both plate reads of the rig already used as their datum (r289: 'the cap rail plus the r215 class bulwark depth of 1.35 m'; r290 registered its datum to r289's fractions), and the plates bracket it without fixing it. On the Brodie anchor plate square on the starboard beam (SLV H99.220/3712, IE40684, 30.6 px/m; build/staging/r289/full-IE40684.jpg; the island's forward end at 3x with a 25-row grid in build/staging/r291/anchor-island-fwd-3x.png, the whole band strip at half scale in anchor-strip-half.png) the painted-ports band on the midship island runs from row 2810 to 2843 (33 px, 1.08 m) and the main-deck cap rail forward and aft of the island reads at rows 2800 (at the main) and 2795 (at the laeisz), 43-48 px (1.40-1.57 m) over the band's foot, which is the main deck's line where the island's side meets the sheer strake (r289 used that foot as the kreuz's deck row and it agreed with rail + 41 px at the main and the laeisz): so the bulwark stands 1.1 m over the deck if the band's top is the cap's own level, and 1.4-1.6 m if the cap rail rows are, and the class 1.35 lies inside that bracket (+/- 0.3 m). On the full-sail halftone (IE32693, 42 px/m at the kreuz, the halftone cell 8 px = 0.19 m; build/staging/r290/sheet-band-2x.png) the band along the hull at the kreuz spans about 55 px, 1.3 m, the same bracket at a coarser scale. NOT READ: the deck's own line, which is behind the bulwark on every plate (freeing ports are not resolved at 30.6 px/m); a general-arrangement drawing (Hamecher 1993, or the Tecklenborg yard's plan) would fix the depth to a decimetre and settle whether the fore and the laeisz stand on the main deck or on an island. COVERING 'wood': the Laeisz practice of a planked weather deck over steel, as on the preserved Peking (1911); not read for Preussen herself. The bulwark's inboard face is the plating's back, bare: a steel bulwark is plating stiffened by bulwark stays with pin rails on the stays, and neither the stays nor the pin rails are drawn (r291; the r276 stanchions and timber pin rail are the WOODEN bulwark's and are not given to a steel ship), so every fall of her running rigging still ends at the deck edge. NOT DRAWN, named: bulwark stays, pin rails, freeing ports. The islands (forecastle, midship bridge, poop) that every plate shows are drawn from r292 (hull.islands).
preussen.hull.mastProvenance: Deck-to-truck 58 m and keel-to-truck 68 m are ATTESTED (de.wikipedia Preußen (Schiff, 1902) infobox: "Masthöhe: 68 m (Kiel-Flaggenknopf), 58 m (Deck-Flaggenknopf)") — one figure for all five masts, because the Laeisz Standardrigg cut interchangeable spars; lower masts and topmasts were one steel tube, only the topgallant stenge fids above. Course yard 32 m and royal 16 m attested in the same source ("Länge Großrah: 32 m; Royalrah: 16 m") — the royal's 0.50 share of the course is the drawn plan's own fraction, an independent cross-check. The lower-mast lengths behind the drawn stack are DERIVED from truckM in hull.js; no lower-mast length is attested in reach. A per-mast spar table (Hamecher 1993) would beat the single figure if it surfaces. r289: the attested 58 m is read as the MAIN mast's, the tallest; the State Library of Victoria's Brodie plate of her at anchor square on the beam (H99.220/3712, IE40684, 30.6 px/m; the read in each mast's yardFracsProvenance) puts the other four trucks lower at one scale - fore 55.8, kreuz 57.1, laeisz 53.1, jigger 46.6 m over the deck, +/- 0.5 m - so those four truckM figures are DERIVED from the plate as ratios to the main's attested figure, and the 'interchangeable spars' sentence above covers the spars, not the poles' heights.
preussen.hull.islands.provenance: READ, r292, off the Brodie anchor plate square on the starboard beam (SLV H99.220/3712, IE40684, 5421 px, bow at the left; build/staging/r289/full-IE40684.jpg; the read in build/staging/r292/read-islands.py, the crops bow-2x.png, island-aft-2x.png, stern-2x.png, fwdwell-2x.png with a 25-row grid). The hull's top edge was traced per column as the first 12-row run darker than 105 of 255 walking down rows 2500-3050, median-filtered over 15 columns; the stem head stands at column 894 and the stern end at 5063, 4169 px over the attested 134 m overall, 31.1 px/m along the hull (r289's rig scale is 30.6, 1.7% apart; heights below use 30.6 and r291's datum, row 2843 = the main deck line = 3.65 m over the water, so they share the rig reads' frame). Columns become u through the loft's deck-level line (MAPPING REVISED, r294, below); r292 mapped them linearly, u = -0.046 + (col - 894) / (31.1 x 124), which is that line only between the forefoot and the run. THREE ISLANDS, each a run where the top edge stands well over the main deck's own top (rows 2819-2839 in the wells): the FORECASTLE from the stem to a vertical light-to-dark edge at column 1293 (12.8 m from the stem head, u 0.075 through the loft's line, 0.057 by r292's linear mapping; the 105-threshold trace drops off the forecastle's top from column 1212, so the break is bracketed 10.2-12.8 m and the vertical edge is taken), its top at row 2702 at the stem falling to about 2740 at the break (8.25 -> 7.05 m over the water; the model's own bow sheer is flatter than the plate's, which is why the top is recorded at both ends and not as one height over the sheer); the MIDSHIP BRIDGE from column 2728 to 3482 (24.2 m, u 0.429-0.625), its top at rows 2750-2765 (6.36-6.69 m, recorded flat at 6.45 +/- 0.3; the per-50-column trace runs 2763, 2763, 2756, 2752, 2754, [the kreuz], 2748, 2752, 2749, 2721, 2721, 2756, 2765, 2765, the 2721 pair a house on the island's top), with the painted-ports band along its side at rows 2810-2843 and the kreuz mast at column 3044 (u 0.511) inside it; and the POOP from a break bracketed between columns 4556 (the trace's first raised run) and 4640 (the band's start and a vertical structure on the stern-2x crop), taken at 4600 +/- 40 (14.9 +/- 1.3 m from the stern end, u 0.900 +/- 0.01 through the loft's line, 0.915 by r292's linear mapping), to the stern, its top at row 2760 near the break falling to 2775 at the stern (6.35 -> 5.85 m over the water; the per-50-column trace aft of the jigger runs 2748, 2759, 2774, 2765, 2771, 2780, 2772). Separately from these three, a short dark run at columns 2595-2643 forward of the bridge island and one at 2684-2703 are deckhouses on the main deck and are NOT recorded. Every top is +/- 0.3 m: +/- 8 rows on the trace and the 2% scale difference. DECK BEHIND EACH TOP: derived, the top less railM 1.0 m (a class figure: the figures standing on the bridge island's top on island-aft-2x.png have the edge at the waist), not read. MASTS: every mast's truckM and yard fractions were read over the MAIN deck line (r289-r291), so every mast still steps on the main deck and the kreuz passes through the bridge island's deck at its station, which is where the plate puts it; nothing in the rig moves. THE BOWSPRIT springs from the forecastle deck (its heel at the forecastle's deck at u 0.02), as on the plate, where it leaves the stem head above the forecastle's top. NOT READ: which fittings stand on each island (the bridge island carries a house on its top and boats on skids; the poop a companion and the wheel), the forecastle's own sheer beyond the two end reads, the mast stations (read in r293 off the same plate, hull.stationRead: the fore at u 0.103, 4.3 m abaft the forecastle's break, the jigger at 0.873, 4.0 m forward of the poop's). MAPPING REVISED, r294 (0y115): the loft places every deck-level station on x(u) = (u - 0.5) lwl + rake(u), which is linear in u only between the forefoot (0.2) and the run (0.72); inside them the two overhangs are absorbed quadratically, so at deck level u 0 is the stem head (x = -67.7 m in hull space) and u 1 the stern end (+66.3), and a plate distance from the head must be solved through that line (hull.stationRead.mapping; the solve in build/staging/r294/apply-record-edits.py). The forecastle's break, 12.8 m abaft the head (column 1293), is u 0.075 on that line (0.057 linearly); the poop's, 14.9 m from the stern end (column 4600, +/- 40), is u 0.900 (0.915 linearly); the bridge island lies in the linear middle and its 0.429-0.625 did not move. Each island now carries its two columns (cols; the forecastle's fore end the stem head's column, the poop's aft end the stern end's) and the block the plate's datum (islands.plate), so the audit reads each built end against the plate and not against a mapping. WHAT r292 DREW: the builder placed the islands at (u - 0.5) lwl as well, so the two errors did not cancel at the ends - the forecastle's wall began 6.2 m abaft the stem head and ran 6.6 m (measured, r293/measure-after.out) where the plate reads 12.8, its wall standing up to 5.5 m abaft the shell's own sheer inside the forefoot; the poop stopped 4.8 m short of the stern end and ran 10.0 m for the plate's 14.9. From r294 the builder places every island station on the loft's line. The bounds are the columns' own: the forecastle's break bracketed 1212-1293 (10.2-12.8 m; the vertical edge taken), the poop's 4560-4640 (+/- 1.3 m), the stem head's column bracketed 830-894 under the headgear (r293), every distance from it 0-2.1 m short. TOPS AS NUMBERS, r298: each island now carries topRead (its rows, the datum rows and height, and the scale), so the audit recomputes every topM from the plate's rows.
preussen.hull.stationProvenance: PLATE READ, r293: the five masts' stations and rakes off the Brodie anchor plate of her at anchor square on the starboard beam (SLV H99.220/3712, Rosetta IE40684, 5421 px, 30.6 px/m by the rig, 31.1 px/m along the hull; build/staging/r289/full-IE40684.jpg; the read in build/staging/r293/r293_refine.py, each mast's foot at 3x in foot-*-3x.png). METHOD: each pole is the dark run crossing a 3-row band every 10 rows from row 1500 down to 15 px above the hull's own top edge at that column; its column is the midpoint of the run's half-depth edges (a darkness-weighted centroid rode the aft half of every pole, where the shroud gang stands, 3-14 px aft of the midpoint); rows crossed by a yard, a top or a doubling (a run wider than 45 px) are skipped; a line is fitted through 67-92 reads per mast (sd 5-11 px); the STATION is where that line meets the main-deck row 2843 (r291's datum, the painted-ports band's foot, 3.65 m over the water), the RAKE is its slope. COLUMNS at the deck row: fore 1428, main 2213, kreuz 3012, laeisz 3799, jigger 4477, +/- 12 px (0.4 m), the spread between the two fits; abaft the stem head (column 894, r292's trace) at 31.11 px/m along the hull: 17.2 / 42.4 / 68.1 / 93.4 / 115.2 m. MAPPING: the loft's deck-level line is not linear in u at the ends. At deck level u 0 is the stem head (x = -lwl/2 - stemRake x loa = -67.7 m in hull space) and u 1 the stern end (+66.3 m); between the forefoot (0.2) and the run (1 - 0.28) x = (u - 0.5) x 124, and inside them the two overhangs are absorbed quadratically, x(u) = (u - 0.5) x 124 - 5.71 x ((0.2 - u)/0.2)^2 forward, + 4.29 x ((u - 0.72)/0.28)^2 aft (hull.js hullSurface.rake, the line every mast foot is placed on). Each pole's distance abaft the stem head is placed at that x and the station solved through that line (stationRead.mapping; the solve in r293/apply-record-edits.py): fore 0.103, main 0.296, kreuz 0.503, laeisz 0.707, jigger 0.873, +/- 0.003 from the column alone. A linear mapping, u = -0.046 + (col - 894)/(31.11 x 124), gives 0.092 and 0.883 at the two ends and the loft draws those 1.7 m and 1.3 m off the plate (the first r293 record was built that way and measured so); r292's islands were mapped linearly and carry that error at their ends (the forecastle's break drawn 9.9 m abaft the head against the plate's 12.8, the poop's 12.8 m from the stern against 14.9) - named (0y115). Before r293 the stations were 0.16 / 0.34 / 0.52 / 0.70 / 0.86, a class placement at 0.18 intervals with no provenance, and the loft drew them 25.3 / 47.9 / 70.2 / 92.5 / 113.4 m abaft the head: the fore stood 8.2 m and the main 5.5 m abaft the plate's poles, the kreuz 2.1 m abaft, the laeisz 0.9 m and the jigger 1.8 m forward of them. The spacing at the deck row is 785 / 799 / 788 / 678 px, 0.203 / 0.207 / 0.204 / 0.176 of lwl (r289's 796 / 796 / 770 / 702 were taken at one height on raked poles and were not used for the stations). RAKE: every mast leans aft, 1.8 / 2.4 / 2.1 / 2.0 / 2.4 degrees, +/- 0.5 (the centroid fit read 1.9-2.9), on a plate whose waterline is level within 10 rows over 2900 columns (the hull's bottom edge at rows 2960-2970 from column 1500 to 4400), so the lean is the ship's and not the plate's; before r293 the five masts stood plumb. WHAT THE MAPPING LEANS ON, named: (1) the stem head's column. r292's trace found the forecastle's top edge from column 894; the bow crop at 2x (ends-bow-2x.png) shows the hull's dark top reaching forward under the headgear to about column 830, so the bow end is bracketed 830-894 and every u by this mapping is 0.0-2.1 m short at the fore mast, less aft: 894 is kept so that the stations and r292's islands keep their distances from each other and from the islands' own reads. (2) The model's overhangs. The mapping fixes the stem head and the stern end to the model's own rake figures (5.7 m and 4.3 m, class figures with no provenance); on the plate the stem meets the water about 4.5 m abaft its head (columns 815-840 at the forecastle top, 955 at the water, +/- 0.5 m). Every u read by the extent mapping (the islands, these stations) keeps its distance from the ends and not from the waterline. NOT MOVED: every truckM and every yard fraction (r289, r290) was read as rows on each pole's own column and stands; the kreuz still stands inside the bridge island (u 0.429-0.625) and passes through its deck; on the plate the fore mast stands 4.3 m abaft the forecastle's break and the jigger 4.0 m forward of the poop's, and against the islands as r292 drew them 7.3 m and 6.1 m (0y115). With the rake the 58 m the card prints is the stack's length along the axis; the plate's rows read it vertically, 0.05 m shorter at 2.4 degrees, inside the read's +/- 0.5 m.

great-eastern.hull.deck.provenance: RECORDED: the contemporary descriptions carry it twice over - Description and History of the Great Eastern (1861): 'the massive wrought-iron deck is covered with teak planking', and of the cellular structure, 'the deck, which is of teak planking placed over the top plates, forms the upper surface of the tube'. The deck beneath is Brunel's double cellular iron top on the Britannia-bridge principle, two half-inch plates top and bottom on longitudinal webs (Descriptive Particulars of the Great Eastern Steam Ship, 1857) - so the teak is a covering laid over iron, which is what this model draws. No plank dimensions are attested; the drawn planks are class defaults.
great-eastern.hull.deck.roofsProvenance: Her two tiers are the same weather deck stepped, within the same laid-deck specification.
great-eastern.hull.masts[0].furlStowProvenance: UNREAD, r310: no plate of this hull furled has been read for how this sail is stowed. The builder lowers the gaff onto a roll along the boom, a schooner's stowage; that is the default named, not a read. A plate of her at anchor that shows this mast between the deck and the top settles it: a gaff standing at its working angle with the sail gathered against the mast is 'brailed'; no gaff aloft is 'lowered'.

great-eastern.hull.paddleProvenance: RECORDED: Lindsay, History of Merchant Shipping and Ancient Commerce IV (1876), specification table - number of floats to each wheel 30, length of floats 13 ft, width of floats 3 ft, weight of each wheel 90 tons; independently 'The paddlewheels were 56 feet in diameter, with 30 floats, each 13 feet broad and 3 feet deep' (Steam Navigation, A.D. 1859-70). Breadth over the paddle boxes 120 ft and over the wheels 118 ft (NYT 30 Jun 1860 detailed description; Shipping Wonders of the World). No float curvature is attested - a float is 'the propelling boards fixed on the radiating arms' (Young's Nautical Dictionary, 1863), a flat board, so its flat form IS the record. Board thickness unattested; the drawn 0.10 m is a class default. Drawn as built; the 1861 replacement wheels (50 ft, narrower floats) are not modelled.

titanic.hull.masts[0].crowsNest.provenance: PLATE READ, r296: the crow's nest off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). The plan draws it as a box on the fore side of the foremast, its top on row 470, its foot on row 490, reaching from the mast's fore edge at column 3138.5 to column 3153.5. The plan's waterline stands on row 823.4 at that column, so the box stands 25.6 to 27.1 m over the water and reaches 1.15 m forward of the mast. The read is good to about 2 rows (0.15 m). The model had hung it at two thirds of the mast, 44.9 m over the water, which was a class rule with no source.
titanic.hull.masts[0].truckProvenance: PLATE READ, r300: the foremast's truck off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). The plan draws each mast as two tapering edges ending in a black knob, the truck, with a house flag flying from it. The mast's centre line (r296's fit, leaning 10.4 degrees on the page) was followed up to the highest row with ink within 3 px of it: row 32 at column 3050.9. The plan's waterline stands on row 824.1 at that column, so the truck stands 60.81 m over the load waterline at 13.03 px/m. The plan's bar scale reads 1% longer, which puts the bound at about 0.6 m; the read itself is good to about a row (0.1 m). The pole is not recorded: the builder draws it from the deck at its foot up to this height, so it follows the deck when the deck moves. Until r300 both poles carried a heightM of 52.2 m from the deck, set to put the trucks at the record's 62.5 m (mastTopM), which stood the fore truck at 63.25 m once r299 raised the deck under it.
titanic.hull.masts[1].truckProvenance: PLATE READ, r300: the mainmast's truck off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). The plan draws each mast as two tapering edges ending in a black knob, the truck, with a house flag flying from it. The mast's centre line (r296's fit, leaning 9.8 degrees on the page) was followed up to the highest row with ink within 3 px of it: row 35 at column 690.5. The plan's waterline stands on row 841.0 at that column, so the truck stands 61.87 m over the load waterline at 13.03 px/m. The plan's bar scale reads 1% longer, which puts the bound at about 0.6 m; the read itself is good to about a row (0.1 m). The pole is not recorded: the builder draws it from the deck at its foot up to this height, so it follows the deck when the deck moves. Until r300 both poles carried a heightM of 52.2 m from the deck, set to put the trucks at the record's 62.5 m (mastTopM), which stood the fore truck at 63.25 m once r299 raised the deck under it.
titanic.hull.funnelTopRead.provenance: RECORDED, r297: the funnel heads stand 42.80 m over the load waterline. Harland and Wolff's figures for the class give 175 ft (53.34 m) from the keel to the top of the funnels and a load draught of 34 ft 7 in (10.54 m); the difference is 42.80 m. CHECKED against the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', bow at the right). Each funnel's head is drawn with its top edge square to the raked stack. That edge was fitted as a line and read where r296's fit of the stack's axis meets it: rows 280.8, 280.7, 281.1 and 289.4, which over the plan's tilted waterline (row 845 at the stern to row 820 at the bow) stand 41.96, 42.22, 42.45 and 42.06 m, mean 42.17 m. At the plan's length scale (13.03 px/m, from her 269.1 m overall) that is 0.63 m under the record. The plan's own bar scale is 1% longer and gives 42.58 m. At funnel 3 the plan's keel line lies on row 971, 10.53 m under its waterline, which matches the recorded draught. WHY THE MODEL WAS LOW: funnelH (19.0 m, the 62 ft funnel height the specification sources print) was built up from the boat deck, which puts the heads at 38.87 m. The record's waterline-to-boat-deck figure is 60 ft 6 in (18.44 m), so the heads stand 24.4 m over the boat deck. The 62 ft is therefore not measured from the boat deck, and the sources that print it do not say what it is measured from. The builder now solves each stack's height from its own deck to funnelTopM, so the head lands at the recorded height whatever the deck under it.
titanic.hull.deck.provenance: RECORDED: the Olympic-class record as the archive compilations carry it (GG Archives; Titanic Connections; both citing The Shipbuilder's 1911 Olympic and Titanic special number) - yellow pine laid on the exposed decks, including the boat deck; pitch pine on the forecastle, poop and well decks; teak only as margin and trim around houses and fittings. Planks 5 in wide by 3 in thick - 127 x 76 mm. The pitch-pine ends and the teak margins are finer distinctions than this one-covering model draws.
titanic.hull.deck.roofsProvenance: The Shipbuilder 1911 names the exposed decks INCLUDING the boat deck, so the tier roofs are inside the same specification as the weather deck.
titanic.hull.islands.provenance: READ, r295, off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic printed in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png; the read in build/staging/r295/r295_read.py). SCALE: the stem head stands at column 3629 and the stern end at 123.5, 3505.5 px apart, which at the recorded 269.1 m overall is 13.027 px/m. The plan's own bar scale reads 3.93 px/ft, which would make her 271.7 m, so every length below carries a bound of 1%. COLUMNS: each break is a curved plate, so its column is the midpoint of the curve's top and foot: the forecastle's break 3113 and 3100, the bridge's fore end 2910 and 2924, its after end 765 and 757, the poop's break 550 and 563 (each good to about 7 px, 0.5 m). LENGTHS on the plan: forecastle 40.1 m, forward well 14.6 m, bridge 165.5 m, after well 15.7 m, poop 33.2 m. The lengths this record carried before r295 were 128 ft (39.0 m), about 50 ft (15.2 m), 550 ft (167.6 m), about 50 ft and 106 ft (32.3 m); they had set the house 2.7 m too far aft at its fore end and 4.8 m too far aft at its after end. MAPPING: each column's distance abaft the stem head is placed at x = stemHeadX + that distance and the island's u is solved through the loft's deck-level line x(u) = (u - 0.5) lwl + rake(u). The house's two stations stay x / lwl, which is how linerHouse reads a tier pin. HEIGHTS, READ r298 (build/staging/r298/r298_read.py, read.json). The plan labels its decks at the stem: BOAT DECK, A, B, C, D, E, F and LOWER, each label standing just above its own line. C, D, E, F and LOWER are the five dashed lines at rows 666, 701, 737, 770 and 803 at column 3500, 2.7 m apart; the forecastle's deck is at the B label. Each island's deck edge is the solid bottom line of the open-rail band drawn along it. That line was traced column by column (the forecastle on columns 3135-3615, the poop on 128-544, every 4 columns, rms 0.32 and 0.34 px about a quadratic) and read over the plan's tilted waterline (row 845 at the stern end to row 820 at the stem head) at 13.03 px/m. FORECASTLE: 15.26 m over the water at the stem head (row 621.2) and 13.61 m at the break (row 646.4); the model drew 13.86 and 13.45, 1.40 m low at the stem. POOP: 12.99 m at the break (row 672.7) and 13.61 m at the stern end (row 667.7); the model drew 13.35 and 13.56. The builder draws each top as a straight line between its two ends; the plan's line is curved, and the straight line lies 0.2 m over it at the worst point of the forecastle (20.1 m abaft the stem head) and 0.08 m over it on the poop. The heights carry the plan's 1% scale bound (0.15 m at 15 m) and about 0.1 m of line width. WHAT r295 READ AS THE WELL DECK: the heavy solid line through both wells, 11.6 m over the water at column 3020 and 11.4 m at column 660. It is the top of the wells' bulwark: the freeing ports drawn in the wells hang from it down to the dashed C line, and the cranes' pedestals are drawn standing on it because the bulwark hides their feet. The well deck is the C line, 10.62 m over the water at column 3020 and between 10.0 and 10.5 m at column 660 (two lines there, not yet told apart). The model's weather deck is 10.1 m amidships rising to 10.85 m at the ends, so it is about 0.3 m low in the fore well; the plan's C deck falls to 9.5 m amidships under the house, so the plan's sheer is about 2.4 m forward against the model's 0.75 m. That sheer is not changed here.
titanic.hull.islands.wellsProvenance: READ, r303, off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png, 13.03 px/m). The plan draws each well's bulwark top as a heavy solid line, 4 to 5 px thick, running from the raised end's break to the house. Each line was traced every 3 columns as the centre of its dark run (the forward well on columns 2930 to 3090, 53 points; the after well on 565 to 760, 66 points; build/staging/r303/r303_trace.py), fitted as a straight line in the column (rms 0.32 and 0.35 px, about 0.03 m), and read at each well's two ends over r297's tilted waterline. The ends are the forecastle's and poop's recorded breaks (islands.list) and the house's stations (houseAt), placed on the plan through the loft's deck-level line (r303_read.py). The line's own thickness, 0.3 to 0.4 m, bounds where in it the plating's top edge lies; the centre is recorded. The forward well's top falls from 11.84 m at the forecastle break to 11.39 m at the house, the after well's rises from 11.30 m at the house to 11.57 m at the poop. The rectangles the plan draws under the line in both wells are the wash ports (portsProvenance, r307). r311 stored each well's raw trace in topRead.trace and refitted both on columns where the line is whole. At the after well's house end, columns 754 to 760, the heavy line ends and r303's trace stepped 3 rows down onto the house's own 2-row line. At the forward well's house end, column 2932, the line thins to 2 rows where it meets the house. Dropping those four points moves each end's top by 0.01 m or less (r303 read 11.84 and 11.40 m forward, 11.29 and 11.58 m aft), and the fits' rms falls from 0.32 and 0.35 px to 0.24 and 0.19 px.
titanic.hull.islands.portsProvenance: READ, r307. Position and size off the 1911 side plan (Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911, build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png, 13.03 px/m): each well's bulwark line has two rectangles hanging under it, found as the columns where a dark edge runs down through rows 4 to 9 under the line (forward well 2963-3010 and 3049.5-3099, 3.6 and 3.8 m; after well 572.5-614.5 and 658-705.5, 3.2 and 3.65 m). Each port's top is the underside of the bulwark line and its bottom the centre of its lower edge, read over the tilted waterline at the port's middle column. In the forward well the bottoms stand 0.05 to 0.07 m under the deck, inside one pixel (0.08 m), so those ports open to the deck. In the after well they stand 0.35 to 0.44 m over the C deck, whose dashed line the plan draws 5 to 6 rows (about 0.4 m) under their lower edges; the model cuts them where the plan draws them and leaves the sill. (r307 had them 0.66 and 0.76 m over the deck, on r299's trace, which ran 0.3 m low there; r309 re-traced it.) Columns map to u linearly between each well's two loft-mapped ends (r303). WHAT THEY ARE, off Bob Read, 'Open Wash Ports of Titanic's Forward Well Deck' (rms-titanic.fr/otb/glossaire/titanic_open_wash_ports.pdf): wash ports to drain a sea off the well; Olympic was built with doors hinged to open outboard in both wells; Titanic's forward doors were removed during fitting out (her Southampton photographs show the white of the well through them) and each open port has two horizontal safety bars; the after well kept its doors. The plan shows the starboard side; the port side is taken as its mirror. The bars' heights (a third and two thirds of the opening) are not read off any plate. The inboard white is Read's 'white painted areas of the well deck', a colour taken from his description, not measured off a photograph.
titanic.hull.stationProvenance: PLATE READ, r296: the two masts' stations off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). Each mast is drawn on the plan as two tapering edges. Both edges were traced every 2 rows from row 430 to row 598 and fitted as lines (rms 0.2 to 0.4 px), and the mast's centre line is their mean. The centre line is read at the height of the model's own mast foot over the plan's waterline, which tilts from row 845 at the stern to row 820 at the bow: the fore at column 3171.1, the main at column 806.5. The scale is the plan's 13.03 px/m over her recorded 269.1 m. The plan's bar scale reads 1% longer, so these distances carry a bound of 1%, and the read itself about 4 px (0.3 m). The plan's mast centre lines lean 10.4 and 9.8 degrees on the page. Taking out the 0.41 degrees by which the plan's waterline is tilted leaves 10.0 and 9.4, so the record keeps its attested rake of 2 inches to the foot (9.46 degrees).
titanic.hull.funnelRead.provenance: PLATE READ, r296: the four funnels' stations off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). Each funnel's two edges were read on rows 304 to 345, in the plain head of the stack above the guys, and their midpoints fitted as a line (rms 0.2 px). The line is read at 19.0 m over the plan's waterline, the height of the stack's root in the model: columns 2648.4, 2177.2, 1713.9 and 1254.4, which stand 75.3, 111.4, 147.0 and 182.3 m abaft the stem head. The spacing is 36.2, 35.6 and 35.3 m. funnelAt is x / lwl, which is how buildFunnel places a stack. The scale carries the plan's 1% bound.
titanic.hull.sheerRead.provenance: PLATE READ, r299, RE-TRACED r309: the C deck (the shelter deck, which ran her whole length and was the floor of both well decks) off the side plan of Olympic and Titanic in Engineering vol. 91, 26 May 1911 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Olympic and Titanic Side Plan 1911.png', 3803 x 1052 px, bow at the right; build/staging/r295/plates/side-plan-1911.png). The plan labels its decks beside the stem, and the C label stands just above a dashed line at row 661 at column 3600. That line was followed aft every 10 columns to column 150 (346 points, each the darkness peak of a 40-column window no more than 1.5 rows from the last point; the line's steepest real slope is 1 row in 10 columns), and fitted as a quintic in the column (rms 0.60 px, about 0.05 m). Each station's height is the fit's row read over r297's waterline, which tilts from row 845 at the stern end (column 123.5) to row 820 at the stem head (column 3629), at 13.03 px/m. The columns map to u through the loft's deck-level line, as r295 placed the islands. Beyond the trace (columns 3600 and 150) each end station holds the fit's end value. The deck stands 12.3 m over the water at the stem, 10.7 m at the forecastle break, 9.57 m amidships, lowest at 9.51 m at u 0.60, 10.02 m in the after well (u 0.85) and 10.5 m at the stern. The builder draws the sheer as a monotone cubic through these stations. trace holds the raw rows, so the fit can be checked against them. BOUNDS: the plan's scale carries 1% (0.1 m at 10 m), the line's width about 0.1 m, and the waterline's tilt is r297's read. WHAT r299 READ WRONG: r299's trace let each point move 4 rows from the last. At column 790, under the house 3 m forward of its after end, a solid line begins 5 to 6 rows (about 0.4 m) under the dashed C line and runs aft under the after well and the poop to the stern; the trace stepped down onto it and followed it to column 150, while its provenance said it followed the dashed line. That put the deck 0.27 m low in the after well, 0.37 m low at u 0.90 and 0.4 m low at the stern, and its rms was 1.20 px where this trace's is 0.60. The solid line is not identified; it is not C, which the plan draws dashed along the whole length. In the after well the plan draws three things close together: the wash ports' lower edges at rows 704 to 706, the dashed C deck at 710 to 711, and that solid line at 715 to 717. The heavy solid line 1.2 to 1.8 m over C, from 11.6 m at the forecastle break through 10.9 m amidships to 12.3 m at the stern, is the top of the shell and of the wells' bulwark (r303), not a deck.
titanic.hull.deckMProvenance: DERIVED, r299, r309: the boat deck's recorded 19.0 m over the water less the C deck's read 9.57 m amidships (sheerRead), over the 3 decks the house stands above C (B, A and the boat deck): 3.143 m. It was 2.96 m while the model drew the deck at 10.1 m amidships, and 3.133 m on r299's read of 9.60 m.
titanic.hull.mastTopMProvenance: CONTESTED. 62.5 m is 'approximately 205 ft above the maximum load line', the round figure that secondary accounts of her fitting-out in August 1911 give for the tops of both masts, with no drawing or measurement cited. The 1911 side plan in Engineering draws the two trucks at different heights: the fore at 60.81 m and the main at 61.87 m over its waterline (r300; each mast carries its read as truckWLM). The masts are built to the plan's reads. This figure is kept as the printed one, and the audit holds the tallest built mast within 1.5 m of it.
titanic.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *RMS Titanic* (read 2026-11-24, r301), Power: three main engines, the two reciprocating engines 30,000 hp combined and the turbine 16,000 hp; 29 boilers (24 double-ended, 5 single-ended), 159 furnaces; over 600 tonnes of coal a day shovelled by 176 firemen. That the turbine ran on the reciprocating engines' exhaust steam is the standard description of the Olympic class's combination machinery; the quoted passage states the engines and outputs, not the steam path.
titanic.hull.capProvenance: BOUNDED, r307. The capping is the heavy line the 1911 side plan draws along each well's bulwark top: 4 px thick at 13.03 px/m, 0.31 m (build/staging/r307/ports.json, lineThickM). The plan draws each wash port's top edge against that line's underside, so the capping is no deeper than the line; before this round the class section B x 0.0256 made it 0.72 m and it would have hung over the top 0.4 m of every port. The capping's own profile is not read.

usv.hull.rakeProvenance: Generated type record: the card's '~22 m' and the lwl 20.5 are composite figures for the survey-USV class (Saildrone's current sheet gives Surveyor 20 m; earlier Surveyor material said 72 ft). The 1.5 m allowance is filled at the authored 3:1 bow:stern character of the type's raked-stem hulls - authored and qualitative, not attested to the centimetre; drawn planking spans 22.00 exactly.
usv.hull.machineryProvenance: Her own card in this record (Saildrone and NOAA survey programmes): a Saildrone is driven by wind and sunlight; the model's hull.wingSail and the stage-6 parts (wing sail, tail vane, solar array, instrument mast).

clipper.hull.masts[0].yardFracsProvenance: CLASS, r285: no plate of this ship has been read for where her yards hang; the course is crossed at the plan's class 0.36 of the truck, which is the silence named, not a read. Above it the yards hang from the mast's own sections (r316, 0y150): the lower topsail yard is fixed on the lower cap, as Howes' rig fixes it, and each hoisting yard is set atrip, at 0.88 of the section it rides (Falconer 1769, ATRIP: 'hoisted up to the mast-head, or to their utmost extent'); a topgallant and a royal on one pole divide its run over the cap below in two equal parts. A broadside plate at 10 px/m or better with the cap rail in it reads a fixed yard's fraction to +/- 0.03.
clipper.hull.masts[0].mastHeightsProvenance: RECORD, r318 (0y154): Cutty Sark's tea rig, fore: top 18.8, topgallant 29.8, royal 39.6 m over the deck. Lubbock, The Log of the Cutty Sark (1924), Appendix III, the spar plan of the tea rig, as tabulated in metres by J. Sankey, 'The Ship Cutty Sark' (johnsankey.ca/cuttysark.html, 'compared to the original lengths quoted in The Log of the Cutty Sark'; saved as build/staging/r318/dl/sankey.html) and by Wikipedia's 'Mast specifications' table, which cites the same appendix. The appendix itself is a fold-out that the archive.org OCR does not read (build/staging/r318/dl/bwb.txt), so the figures are Sankey's conversion of it. Lubbock's text checks the main: 'Her mainmast from load line to truck was 151 feet in length' (46.0 m; bwb.txt line 2196), which leaves 1.5 m from the load line to the deck under a 44.5 m truck. Until r318 the lower mast was a recorded 23.2 m carried up by Steel's 1794 proportions, a topmast 0.60 of it and a topgallant mast half the topmast, which left two yards on a pole sized for one. CONTESTED: the table names each height by a sail (top, topgallant, royal, skysail) and not by a fitting. The builder reads the first as the top's platform, the second as the topmast crosstrees and the last as the truck. If the first is the lower cap instead, every lower mast is 10% shorter than drawn. The fore course yard, 23.8 m, is from the same table; until r318 it was 0.875 of the lower mast. The yards above it keep the plan's shares of it.

clipper.hull.masts[2].furlStowProvenance: READ, r310 (0y¹³⁸): LOWERED. The plate is the State Library of Queensland's John Oxley Library negative 146359, 'The Cutty Sark waiting in Sydney Harbour for the new season's wool', 1885-94 (Commons 'StateLibQld 1 146359 Cutty Sark (ship).jpg', 706 x 1000 px), taken from high on her port quarter at anchor. At the mizzen it is about 11 px/m: 167 px from the poop to the mizzen top. A gaff 0.25 m thick and over 10 m long would show at 3 px by 110 px or more, as her 0.3 m yards do. No gaff stands on the mizzen: the lower mast is bare from the crossjack yard down to the poop, and no brailed bundle lies along its after side. The poop is covered by an awning whose ridge runs aft from the mast at the height a boom would stand. So the gaff is down, either lowered to the boom or struck, and the builder's lowered stowage is the nearer of the two it draws. CONTESTED: this is one plate of one ship, the Cutty Sark whose dimensions this class hull carries, at anchor in port 16 to 25 years after her launch and after her 1880 re-rig. It does not show where the gaff lies, and other clippers may have kept a standing gaff.

dreadnought.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *HMS Dreadnought (1906)* (read 2026-11-24, r301), Propulsion: two paired sets of direct-drive turbines, each driving two propellers; 18 Babcock & Wilcox boilers at 250 psi; 23,000 shp rated; 21.6 kn from 27,018 shp on trials, 9 October 1906; 2,868 long tons of coal and 1,120 long tons of fuel oil sprayed on the coal.

yamato.hull.deck.provenance: RECORDED, species CONTESTED: Skulski (Anatomy of the Ship - The Battleship Yamato) gives hinoki, Japanese cypress, planks 127 x 76 mm; the Yamato Museum, Kure, states the ship's deck timber was Taiwanese cypress. Neighbouring cypresses of the same pale colour class, so the drawn tone stands either way. Plank width 127 mm from Skulski; butt length is a class default.
yamato.hull.deck.roofsProvenance: Her hinoki planking is recorded for the exposed decks, which on a battleship includes the shelter deck the tiers stand on.
yamato.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *Japanese battleship Yamato* (read 2026-11-24, r301), infobox: installed power 12 Kampon boilers, 150,000 shp; propulsion 4 shafts, 4 steam turbines; speed 27 kn.

carrier.hull.rakeProvenance: loa 337.0 is the ship's EXTREME length - 1,106 ft, the figure Commander, Naval Air Force Atlantic gives for USS Gerald R. Ford - and it is not a shell length: the flight deck is its own attested plate at 1,092 x 256 ft (333 x 78 m), and no source publishes the shell's length between extremities. The rakes 0.03/0.02 are reconstruction; the drawn planking spans 333.85, INSIDE the record's loa. The deck is drawn at flightDeckLen 333.0, anchored so the aft round-down overhangs the fantail and the span from the shell's bow tip to the round-down is 337.00 = loa exactly. A planking-only sweep reads -3.15 on this hull by construction; that is the record's geometry, not an under-fill.
carrier.hull.islandSideProvenance: ATTESTED: the Ford's island stands at the starboard deck edge abaft amidships and her landing area is angled to port — the arrangement of every angled-deck carrier, stated in this record's own text and on the class's page (Wikipedia, Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, accessed 2026-08-03). The word drives every one-sided fitting through the builder's islandSide(): the island, the two deck-edge lifts and the hangar doors under them, the catapults, the foul line and the deck park stand on this side, and the landing area runs forward to the other. Until r270 each was drawn at +z under the belief that +z was starboard; +z is port (build/staging/r254/side.json, the frame's own statement at the head of hull.js), so the whole arrangement was the ship's mirror. The audit reads this word and the meshes, not the builder (D-ISLAND-SIDE).
carrier.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier* (read 2026-11-24, r301): two A1B reactors per ship; steam piped to four main turbine generators for ship systems and the EMALS catapults; steam turbines for propulsion; four shafts (infobox).

container.hull.freeboardProvenance: TYPE SHIP — the drawn freeboard is DERIVED, and the card row says so (rule 10). This composite is drawn at the 24,000-TEU generation its own rows name (MSC Gülsün / MSC Irina classes, 399.9 m × 61.3 m): depth moulded 33.2 m to main deck (RINA, Significant Ships of 2019, MSC Gülsün; the Irina class repeats the figure) less the recorded 16.0 m deep draught leaves 17.2 m of weather-deck freeboard. The old 30.0 had no source and stood the deck at nearly the whole moulded depth over the water — a hull floating near her light line drawn as loaded. The statutory summer freeboard is smaller still and is measured to a lower freeboard deck, not the weather deck this model lofts — the same distinction ever-given's stationProvenance records from her casualty report.
container.hull.rakeProvenance: AUTHORED to fill the record's own allowance: loa 399.9 − lwl 383.0 = 16.9 m, and the old 0.03/0.0 drew only 12.0 m of it (r129 fleet sweep, −4.9). 383.0 is the class's length between perpendiculars (RINA, Significant Ships of 2019, MSC Gülsün — the same plate as the depth moulded above); on this generation the transom stands nearly plumb at the aft perpendicular and virtually the whole LOA−LPP difference is the flared bow above the bulb — ever-given, the fleet's attested hull of the same 400 m generation, carried the identical 383 LBP against 399.94 LOA before r113 moved her lwl to her casualty report's 387 waterline. The stern keeps its authored 0.0 and the stem takes the allowance: 0.0423, which the r129 loft clamp trims to 16.90 m of bow overhang, 399.90 m drawn exactly. NOTE the semantics this leaves: this type ship's lwl is the class LBP; the loaded waterline of the real hull runs ~4 m further over the bulb (the ever-given precedent) and is not published for this class, so the record keeps the figure a plate attests.
container.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *Ever Given* (read 2026-11-24, r301): 'As with most large container ships, Ever Given's propulsion system consists of a single low-speed two-stroke diesel engine coupled to a large fixed-pitch propeller.' This record is the type, not one ship, so the card states the type's usual plant.

ever-given.hull.rakeProvenance: The lwl 387.00 this record carries is the LBP her own casualty report states (PMA R-026-2021-DIAM, the same plate stationProvenance reads), and the transom stands near-plumb at the AP on this 400 m generation (sternRake 0 - the class geometry r131 sourced from the MSC Gulsun plate, RINA Significant Ships of 2019). So the whole loa - lwl = 12.98 m allowance is the flared bow above the bulb. stemRake authored 0.0325, a hair over the exact 0.032452; the r129 clamp trims the drawn overhang to 12.98 m so planking spans 399.98 exactly.
ever-given.hull.stationProvenance: Twin-island stations from the ship's OWN papers, not a photograph: the PMA casualty report R-026-2021-DIAM carries her voyage-plan particulars (Fig. 6, loading computer) — keel to highest point 75.71 m, air draft 60.26 m at ~15.4 m draught, and the highest point (the bridge mast) 245.35 m forward of the aft perpendicular on LBP 387.00 m, which is u 0.366 from the FP; bridgeU 0.361 lands the drawn mast there. Depth moulded 32.90 m and breadth 58.80 m from the same report's Table 1 (vessel certificates); freeboard 17.2 = depth less the 15.7 m draught (the statutory 10.226 m summer freeboard is to a lower freeboard deck, not the weather deck the model draws). Funnel casing at funnelU 0.845 READ off the GA plan reproduced in the report (Fig. 2, 711x315 px, ~1.04 px/m — good to +/-4 m, no finer), cross-checked against Commons broadsides (kees torn 51343xxx series: dark-green casing amid the stacks, short black stack above). Stow: 23 rows on the real ship; the drawn TEU grid fits 22 across the 58.8 m beam (one row under, below any frame's resolution), 10 tiers on deck midships-aft per the Rotterdam photographs. EVERGREEN side lettering span and stern name from the same photographs; bow name NOT drawn — the flare there is curved and a flat decal would lie about it.
ever-given.hull.machineryProvenance: Wikipedia, *Ever Given* (read 2026-11-24, r301): licence-built Mitsui MAN B&W 11G95ME-C9, 59,300 kW at 79 rpm, service speed 22.8 kn; four Yanmar 8EY33LW auxiliary generators; two 2,500 kW bow thrusters.

azzam.hull.houseProvenance: DERIVED from the delivery photograph: the lowest tier's windows run forward to 0.157 m/px pixel 1010 (u 0.18) and its roof tip lands at u 0.87; the crest's forward face is the block's glass foot (u 0.437) and its full-height wall ends at u 0.66, the continuous-bright edge read at 20.9 m. SUPERSEDED for the house spans and tier edges by housePlateProvenance (round 97, the 8.96 px/m broadside): the 0.87 roof tip this small plate gave is the ensign flying just aft of the real 0.82 roof end, a misread its resolution could not avoid.
azzam.hull.boatsProvenance: INBOARD: her tenders stow in a garage within the hull, not on deck. The design accounts record the concept grew from 145 m to 180.6 m partly to make room for tenders, fuel and machinery inside (Nauta design history via Boat International and YachtBuyer, which lists her tender garage), and the delivery photograph on this card shows a bare topside — no boat stands on any deck. Her tender complement is not published, so no count is claimed.
azzam.hull.cluster.provenance: RE-MEASURED 2026-08-16 off a clean broadside (Wikimedia Commons, File:Azzam IMO 9693367 S Bremen 09-05-2014.jpg, Wolfgang Fricke, CC BY 3.0) with the stem, transom and waterline as the three anchors and her recorded 180.6 m as the scale — 8.33 px per metre. The earlier derivation, off the smaller delivery photograph, put her mast at u 0.542 and 47.2 m over the water; the broadside reads u 0.638 and 36.2 m, which is a sixth of her length and a quarter of her air draught, and drew her with a radio tower amidships. Her house is FOUR decks, not five: the crest reads 21 m over the water against the five-deck stack's 24.25. AFT DOMES CORRECTED 2026-08-17 (round 97): a strip scan at 17.8-23.0 m over the water, anchors x332/x1950/y941 at 8.96 px/m, finds white mass aft of the block only at u 0.700-0.721 (the 3.4 m pair) and 0.731-0.744 (the 2.2 m single) — nothing stands at the earlier 0.763/0.803, which would float past the fairing foot now that tier 2's wall is measured to end there. Their bases stay on the tier-2 roof terrace, which the tierFloorsM correction raises to the 19.5-19.8 m this provenance already reads. The mast u could NOT be re-verified the same way: the yard crane's lattice crosses the 29.5-33 m strip behind her, so 0.638 stands on the r95 read.
azzam.hull.tierBands.provenance: RE-MEASURED 2026-08-17 off the kept broadside (File:Azzam IMO 9693367 S Bremen 09-05-2014.jpg, Wolfgang Fricke, CC BY 3.0) at 8.96 px/m with stem x332 / transom x1950 / waterline y941 as anchors. The glazing is not a continuous ribbon: each tier carries GROUPS of punched lights with long blank wall runs between, different per tier. groups[tier] = [uStart, uEnd, pitchM, pierFrac]; pitchM 0 is one continuous run. Tier 0: six 4.1 m lights at 6.1 m pitch forward, small lights amidships, a 23 m run aft. Tier 1: four 3.2 m lights forward, small lights, a long aft run. Tier 2: a 10 m forward run and a short aft group under the fairing. Crest: the raked front glass and one aft run. AFT EXTENTS CORRECTED round 97: the r96 row scan read dark BACKGROUND over the stepped-down stern as glazing, because with every tier drawn ~3 m the walls were assumed to reach the old aft edges — the silhouette envelope shows tier 0's wall ends at u 0.82, tier 1's at 0.795, tier 2's at the fairing foot 0.744 and the crest's at the block face 0.708, so the groups that ran past those edges (t0 to 0.93, t1 to 0.889, t2 to 0.822, crest to 0.745) are trimmed or dropped. What stands aft of each wall is open terrace, and glazing there is UNKNOWN, not asserted. bandsM[tier] = [sill, head] in metres over the waterline, straight from the plate: 10.9-12.6 / 14.8-16.7 / 18.1-19.5 / 21.2-22.4 — the crest head read 22.8 exceeds the 22.5 roof by less than the read noise and is clipped under it.
azzam.hull.hullRows.provenance: READ 2026-08-17 off the same broadside at 8.96 px/m. The freeboard is not bare: an upper row of ~1.0 m rectangular windows, sills 4.9 m and heads 6.9 m over the waterline, in five clusters at ~1.9 m pitch between u 0.26 and 0.49, with two dark side doors aft of them; a low porthole line, ~0.45 m glasses about 3.0 m over the water, in clusters of three or four between u 0.25 and 0.52 plus one forward at u 0.11; and a long tinted band 8.2-8.7 m over the water under the aft deck edge, broken once, u 0.60-0.77. Heights are placed as fractions of the recorded 9.0 m freeboard, so the rows parallel the deck line as the photograph shows.
azzam.hull.housePlateProvenance: RE-MEASURED 2026-08-17 (round 97) off the kept broadside at 8.96 px/m, by reading the upper silhouette envelope column by column with a ship-white classifier rather than matching window rows. The aft staircase was previously misattributed by two tiers because every tier was drawn ~3 m and the real tiers are 4.5/3.9/2.6/2.5 m: the 0.821 edge is TIER 0's roof end (roof 13.5 m, visible terminating at u 0.819), 0.888 is the main-deck bulwark run-out, and tier 2's wall in fact ends at the fairing foot 0.744. tierFloorsM 13.5/17.4/20.0 and houseTopM 22.5 are the envelope's roof reads, each confirmed at two or more exposed spans fore and aft (tier 0: 13.3-13.7 fore, 13.5-13.8 aft; tier 1: 17.3-17.9 fore, 17.3-17.4 aft; tier 2: white to ~20 under the crest's raked glass; top = blockTopM). The UAE ensign occludes u 0.83-0.87 at 10-15 m; the tier-0 aft edge 0.82 is the roofline's visible termination just forward of it. houseTaper 0.03 stands. Aft of the house the stern terraces down — bulwark tops 9.7 m to u 0.90, then 6.9 (0.905-0.93), 6.3, 5.4, 4.5, 3.1 m at the transom — which the model does not yet build; the read is recorded here for when it does.
azzam.hull.formProvenance: READ off the same broadside at 8.33 px/m (File:Azzam IMO 9693367 S Bremen 09-05-2014.jpg, Wolfgang Fricke, CC BY 3.0). houseRamp: every tier front is raked so its head lands on the next front's foot, one continuous sweep from the foredeck to the crest, where the model had four vertical steps. faired: the topside between the waterline and the sheer is an unbroken gloss surface with no visible plate lands, tone patchwork or streaking anywhere along her 180.6 m. bowFlare 0.14: the topsides lean out over the fine entry; the plate cannot give a number at this bearing, so this is set to the smallest value that reads as flare in the bow capture and is marked DERIVED, not measured. capM 0.2: the dark strip at the deck edge measures 0.11-0.33 m on the broadside (median 0.2) where the model's beam-derived capping drew 0.53 m.
azzam.hull.sternSteps.provenance: MEASURED 2026-08-17 (round 98) off the kept broadside at 8.96 px/m, anchors x332/x1950/y941, silhouette envelope sampled every 0.0025 u (Research/segment-azzam-envelope.py). Aft of the house the stern descends in terraces, and the tops RAKE within each terrace - the silhouette is the outer bulwark cap, sweeping down toward each break: 9.9-9.6 m to the break at u 0.884 (the main-deck bulwark; round 97's coarser sampling read its run-out as 0.888), then 6.9-7.0 to 0.931, 6.6-6.1 to 0.946, 5.7-4.9 to 0.9625, 4.9-4.2 to 0.975, and 3.5-3.0 at the transom (flat 3.0 aft of u 0.9825). Occluders excluded from the read: the ensign u 0.83-0.87, davits or staff at 0.900, 0.9225, 0.930-0.9325 and 0.945-0.9475. topM [fwd, aft] is the measured cap line; deckM is DERIVED as the span's low cap minus a 0.9-1.0 m parapet, because the plate cannot see the decks behind their own bulwarks. The first span's deck is the hull's recorded 9.0 m sheer (deckM absent); its parapet is the 0.6-0.9 m the plate reads above it. ROUND 102: the 0.884 riser (the only full-height drop) now carries a tinted band and centreline doors - the delivery plate reads that face dark against the white, but its ~6.6 px/m cannot place panes, so the ARRANGEMENT is inferred. Twin flights close each lesser break, tops flush with the deck above; they stand behind the next bulwark aft, which is why the broadside envelope never saw them. No pool is drawn: none is attested at any measurable position.
azzam.hull.deck.provenance: RECORDED: the builder's specification as carried by the BOAT International Superyacht Directory entry for Azzam (Lurssen, 2013) - teak deck, steel hull, aluminium superstructure; press copy repeats 2,200 m2 of laid teak. Plank width and butt pattern are CLASS defaults for a yacht's laid teak (90 mm strakes), below what any plate of her can resolve.
azzam.hull.deck.roofsProvenance: TERRACES, NOT THE CREST: the 2,200 m2 of laid teak in the builder-sourced copy is far more area than her weather deck alone can carry on a 180.6 x 20.8 m hull, so her tier terraces carry the rest — which her photographs show. But the crest top is not among them: on the Klaus Jordan delivery-trials aerial (Lurssen press 2013, via CharterWorld wp-content, 960x640 copy, ~4.4 px/m locally at the crest — a colour-field read only, stated in Research/AZZAM-PLATES.md) the roof the radome cluster and mast stand on reads unbroken white coated plate, with the teak one level down on the ringing terraces. Pedestal base-plate detail is below that plate's resolution and is not claimed.
azzam.hull.paintProvenance: MEASURED off two independent broadsides — Wikimedia Commons File:AzzamCadiz.jpg (Javier Virues Ortega, CC BY-SA 4.0, port side, bow left) and File:Yacht Azzam - UAE.jpg (Farid mernissi, CC BY-SA 4.0, starboard, bow right). Both show her WHITE to the waterline with no boot-top and a near-black antifouling, where the class default for a hull built after 1955 is oxide red. And both show the deck edge rising about 3.0 m from amidships to the stem, against the 0.25 m the record carried — which is why she read as a flat slab. The RISE is a difference between two points on one line, so it is immune to where the hull ends and the first tier begins, which is the one thing these plates cannot resolve.
azzam.hull.sheerProvenance: MEASURED 2026-08-25 (round 160) off two independent broadsides, each with its scale: the Cadiz in-service broadside (Commons AzzamCadiz.jpg, 17.27 px/m re-anchored, stem tip x351 y1709, waterline fit y=1847.8+0.00162x) reads the stem head at 8.05-8.13 m and the foredeck cap 8.19-8.38 m rising to 8.84 at the house front; the kept Bremen broadside (azzam-broadside-fricke-2014.jpg, 8.96 px/m, anchors x332/x1950/y941) reads the same stem head at 8.37 m. Both refute the former sheerBow 3.0 (a 12.0 m bow) by ~3.9 m: her sheer is INVERTED, the bow below the freeboard deck, one sweep rising aft into the house. bowTopM is the two-plate band's centre; sheerBow = bowTopM - freeboard. The 1343_Azzam.jpg fitting-out oblique was rejected as a witness: no local scale anchor at the bow (Research/AZZAM-PLATES.md, r160 section).
azzam.hull.machineryProvenance: Her own card in this record (Lürssen; Boat International): roughly 94,000 shp, combined diesel and gas turbine, four waterjets, over 30 kn. Not checked against a builder's specification in r301.

endurance.hull.headProvenance: NO HEAD. The Framnaes longitudinal section (as Polaris, RMG J9266, web copy 1024x322 px, ~16.9 px/m along the hull) draws a straight raked stem, the 1.3 m baulk, with the bowsprit rising from the stemhead and no knee of the head, no headrail and no gammoning slot; Hurley's heeled plate (build/endurance-heeled.png, 1280x995 px, bow-on and foreshortened, so it bounds the shape and gives no station) shows the same plain stem under the bowsprit. The old record's head: 1 drew a pale cutwater knee standing 1.3 m before the stem, an S-curved headrail a side from the bow planking to the knee, and three turns of rope gammoning: an eighteenth-century head on a 1912 polar barquentine, in every bow view. r271 correction; the bowsprit keeps its bobstay.
endurance.hull.masts[0].courseGear.provenance: PLATE READ, r281: Hurley's plate of Endurance under full sail, taken from ahead (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg, 2828x3912; the fore course yard spans ~1440 px of a 1540 px crop, ~90 px/m at the yard), shows on the FORE FACE of the set fore course four buntlines, two a side, leaving the foot at about 0.3 and 0.65 of the half-yard (+/- 0.1) and running up and in across the canvas toward the slings, and each clew garnet leaving its clew for the yard at about half the half-yard (0.50 +/- 0.05) on both sides. The plate stops at the yard: where the falls belay is NOT read from it — the fife rail is the class answer (r280, hull.fifeRail) — and the lead blocks under the top are a class arrangement. A plate of her foredeck from aft would settle the belay; none is in reach (r280).
endurance.hull.masts[0].yardsProvenance: PLATE READ, r282: THREE YARDS - the course, ONE deep topsail and a topgallant. Every plate of this ship that shows the fore mast whole crosses three yards and no fourth. Hurley's plate of her under full sail, taken from ahead (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg, 2828x3912, ~90 px/m at the course yard), sets three square sails: the middle one is a single cloth from its yard down to the course yard's arms, with one reef band across it and no spar across its face. Hurley's night plate (build/hurley-night.jpg, 2590x3502; the fore mast about 2000 px from the course yard to the truck, read at half scale) shows three yards with their sails furled on them; the gaps course-to-topsail, topsail-to-topgallant and topgallant-to-truck read 210 : 230 : 230 px (+/- 10), and the builder's class fractions for a single-topsail list (course 0.36, topsail 0.55, topgallant 0.76 of the truck over the deck; gaps 0.19 : 0.21 : 0.24) agree with them to within the read, so the fractions stand. Hurley's heeled plate (build/endurance-heeled.png, 1280x995) shows three yards. The upper yards' lengths on the full-sail plate are 0.82 (topsail) and 0.55 (topgallant) of the course yard's apparent span, foreshortened by their greater distance from a camera ahead of and below the ship; the class shares 0.88 and 0.68 stand. Until r282 the record listed course, lower topsail, upper topsail and topgallant - Howes' doubled rig, a class list no plate of this ship supports - and the builder crossed a lower topsail yard she never carried and drew her deep topsail as two sails.
endurance.hull.masts[0].upperGear.provenance: PLATE READ, r283: Hurley's plate of Endurance under full sail, taken from AHEAD with the ship beset (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg, 2828x3912; the fore mast's canvas cropped at full resolution in build/staging/r282/plate-mid-1x.png (the topsail, 1790x880) and plate-top-1x.png (the topgallant, 1510x680), the yards' centres at 2x in build/staging/r283/plate-mid-yardcentre-2x.png and plate-top-yardcentre-2x.png; ~70 px/m at the topsail yard and ~55 px/m at the topgallant yard, both farther from the camera than the course yard). TOPSAIL: on the FORE FACE of the set sail a line leaves each clew at the course yard's arm and runs up the canvas to the topsail yard, meeting it 0.15 (starboard, the image's left) and 0.19 (port) of the half-yard out from the mast (+/- 0.05: the yard's half spans ~645 px, the mast ~835 px from the crop's left edge, the lines meet the yard at ~715 and ~930 px) - the CLEWLINES to the quarter blocks; recorded as 0.17. Lines from the foot run up the face and converge on the slings, two a side read as likely and one a side certain, their foot stations not readable within 0.15 of the half-yard at this scale - the BUNTLINES; the class stations 0.30 and 0.65 are kept and named as class figures. TOPGALLANT: a line from each clew to the yard meeting it 0.05-0.14 of the half-yard from the mast (the yard's half ~440 px; the lines meet it 20-60 px from the mast's line); recorded as 0.12, +/- 0.05. From the foot one line a side rises to the slings; its station reads about 0.4 of the half, +/- 0.15. WHAT THE PLATE DOES NOT SHOW: where the falls belay (the deck is out of frame below the course), and the blocks at the yards (the lines vanish into the yard's own line) - the leads and the belays are class figures: the falls over the top's after rim to the fife rail's side pins, the overflow to the bulwark's pin rail. Until r283 the record said nothing of the upper sails' gear and the builder drew none.
endurance.hull.masts[0].reefs.provenance: PLATE READ, r284: Hurley's plate of Endurance under full sail, taken from AHEAD with the ship beset (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg, 2828x3912; the topsail cropped at full resolution in build/staging/r282/plate-mid-1x.png, 1790x880, its two leeches at 2x in build/staging/r284/plate-topsail-leftleech-2x.png and -rightleech-2x.png and the band's middle at 3x in plate-topsail-band-3x.png; ~75 px/m at the band's row, the band spanning ~1105 px from leech to leech). TOPSAIL: ONE reef band, a straight seam across the cloth from (280, 350) at the starboard leech (the image's left) to (1385, 232) at the port leech, with a row of eyelets along it. Its row on each leech: starboard, head at row 75 (the cloth under the yard), band 350, clew 765 - 0.40 of the leech; port, the yard's line extrapolated to row -35 above the crop's edge, band 232, clew 640 - 0.40 of the leech. Recorded as 0.40 of the drop, +/- 0.03 (the camera below and ahead expands the lower cloth by about a tenth over the upper, which moves the read by under 0.01; r282's 'about a third' was an eyeball). THE POINTS: dark blobs along the band's line at a pitch of 51-64 px where no rigging crosses it (338, 389, 443, 500, 557, 614, 672, 731 ... 847, 906, 970 ... 1134, 1197), about 0.77 m at the band's scale, +/- 0.08 - recorded as pitchM 0.77; about 18-19 eyelets across the cloth, the builder placing round(width / pitch). THE BAND'S WIDTH is not readable at this scale (one seam line and the eyelets read, not two tablings): bandM 0.30 is a class figure for a 14 m topsail and is named as such. COURSE: no band reads on the course's fore face at ~90 px/m (build/staging/r284/plate-course-half.png; the r281 read of the buntlines and garnets off the same face saw none) - recorded as none, with the bound that the course is foreshortened from below and a band low on it would lie in the foot's belly. TOPGALLANT: no band on the topgallant's face at ~55 px/m (build/staging/r282/plate-top-1x.png) - recorded as none. Until r284 the builder drew every square sail in the fleet plain and the record said nothing of reef bands.
endurance.hull.masts[0].yardFracsProvenance: PLATE READ, r285: Hurley's beset broadside (RMG P00018, build/hurley-broadside.png, 4800x3743; the ship cropped at 3x with a grid in build/staging/r285/plate-broadside-ship-3x-grid.png and the fore mast at 6x in plate-broadside-foremast-6x-grid.png). SCALE 12.4 +/- 0.4 px/m, from the mast spacing against the record's stations (fore to main 162 px for 0.328 x 39.6 m, main to mizzen 148 px for 0.302 x 39.6 m; the hull's ends are behind ice, so its length gives no better figure), the same for heights because the view is on the beam. AT THE FORE MAST (col 2600): the cap rail's top edge at row 620 +/- 3; the course yard with its furled sail a dark bar about 90 px wide across the mast centred on row 545 +/- 3 (the strongest horizontal feature on the mast; the top and the lowered topsail yard read faintly at rows 495-530); the pole vanishing at row 372 +/- 6 (a darkness of 42 against a sky of 22 at row 380, 24 at 360). With the bulwark 1.35 m (16.7 px) from the plan (r272): the course yard 75 px over the cap = 6.0 m, 7.4 m over the deck; the truck 248 px over the cap = 20.0 m, 21.4 m over the deck; the yard at (75 + 16.7) / (248 + 16.7) = 0.35 +/- 0.03 of the truck over the deck. That is the plan's class fraction (0.36) inside the read's bound, so the plate does NOT move the course yard as (0y88) supposed; recorded as 0.35, the plate's own number, which the builder draws. The topsail's and the topgallant's yards were LOWERED on the beset ship (sails furled), so their set fractions do not read on this plate. From r316 (0y150) they are set atrip, at 0.88 of the section each rides (Falconer 1769, ATRIP), where the plan's 0.55 and 0.76 had hung both inside the doublings, under the cap of the section below. Hurley's full-sail plate from ahead (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg) puts the topsail yard at about 0.57 and the topgallant yard at about 0.93 of the height from the course yard to the truck; the model's are 0.73 and 0.97 (0.31 and 0.63 before r316). That plate is not read into the record: it is taken from low on the ice ahead of her, and its perspective is not solved. The truck row is the read's weakest figure: see trucksContested.
endurance.hull.masts[1].capRead.provenance: Hurley's beset broadside (RMG P00018, build/hurley-broadside.png, 4800x3743), read in r304 by build/staging/r304/r304_steps.py: the darkness of each pole summed across it, row by row, which measures its width where the blur is wider than the spar. The main pole sums to about 260 over rows 425-490 and steps to about 520 below row 500 (the half-way crossing, +/- 3 rows): a thin topmast over a thick lower mast, with the gaff's throat just under the step. The cap rail stands at row 630 (r285) and the deck 16.7 px under it (the plan's 1.35 m bulwark, r272), so the cap is 146.7 px over the deck. The pole fades to half its plateau at row 385 (+/- 6), 261.7 px over the deck, so the cap stands at 146.7/261.7 = 0.56 of the truck. A thin pole may fade before its truck, which makes this share a bound from above. The same read on the fore gives 0.55 for its top against the builder's 0.586 for the fore's stack, so the method lands within 0.04 on a mast whose sections are known. The heeled plate (build/endurance-heeled.png, Commons 4776 px copy in build/staging/r280) shows the mizzen's crosstrees with the topmast standing beside the lower masthead. The plate gives no lengths: the truck stays the record's figure (trucksContested), and only the cap's share of it is read here. Hurley's night plate (August 1915) shows the main ending at a capped head level with the fore topsail yard, which may be a struck topmast; it is not read here.
endurance.hull.masts[1].gaffRead.provenance: Hurley's beset broadside (RMG P00018, build/hurley-broadside.png, 4800x3743), read in r306 by build/staging/r306/r306_gaffread.py (crops plate-gaffs-4x.png): the gaff is a faint line rising aft from the mast, under the cap, with the sail stowed. For every column of its visible run the darkest row in a 13-px band is taken, a line is fitted (weighted by the dip under the sky), and the gaff is read from the mast's axis along that line to its last visible column. The main gaff runs 80.8 px from the mast's axis (column 2766) to its peak at column 2831, row 493.6, at 36.4 degrees over the horizontal (the line fits its rows to 1.48 px). The throat meets the axis at row 541.5, 105.2 px over the deck (the cap rail row of r285 plus the plan's 1.35 m bulwark, 16.7 px, r272). Against the lower mast's 146.7 px from deck to cap (r304's read of the same plate), the gaff is 0.55 of the lower mast and the throat stands at 0.72 of it. Each end is good to about 3 px, so each share to about 0.029. The shares do not depend on the plate's scale, which is contested (trucksContested): the built gaff is this share of the built lower mast. The peak stands a few px over the cap on the plate, as a long gaff's does.
endurance.hull.masts[1].gaffStowProvenance: PLATE READ, r306: the main is a loose-footed sail, brailed in to the mast under a gaff that stays aloft, and she carries no main boom. On Hurley's plate of her under sail from ahead (build/hurley-fullsail.jpg) the square sails are set and no fore-and-aft canvas shows abaft the main mast. The funnel stands 5.5 m abaft the mast (stationProvenance), under the gaff's reach: a sail of this head set on a boom short enough to clear the stack would put its leech through the funnel's top. Where the sheet led when the sail was set is not read; the model draws the sail as both plates show it, brailed.
